A man speaks in a calm voice, "Towing can't always be considered a rescue technique. Sometimes you'll give someone a tow if they're getting tired, or as a safety precaution while crossing an open stretch. Towing is also a great way to deal with an injured or seasick paddler." This is accompanied by soft, acoustic guitar music.
A male voice says, "Whatever the situation, as the rescuer, you have a lot of towing options to choose from," while soft music plays.
A person speaks, "First off, you need to decide on a tow line to buy," accompanied by background music.
A person speaks in a clear, instructional tone, "All toe lines should have a terminal."
A male voice calmly states, "on the end for clipping them on, and a quick-release buckle."

A man speaks, "that lets you break free with a simple flick of your wrist." Another man says, "The leash portion of a tow system can be short or long. Short ones around 5 to 10 feet are called cowtails and are better for quick and short use." The sound of rushing water can be heard throughout.

A person says, "Longer leashes are usually around 30 to 45 feet and are better for towing over a long distance." Another person says, "There are many different ways to use a tow line, but we don't have time to cover all of them. So here are some of our favorites." A third speaker says, "The inline tow is the most basic towing system."
A person speaks, "and simply involves the towboat clipping onto the bow of the boat to be towed."
A person speaks, "You'll want to use a tow line with some stretch, like a cowtail, and the boat being towed."

A male speaker says, "should be far enough behind so that its bow won't bump into the tow boat. You can also add a second tow boat to the front of the line for additional speed and power. A contact tow is a great fast tow for short distances, such as getting clear of surf zones," all while soft background music plays.

A male voice says, "The paddler to be towed grabs a hold of the rescuer's foredeck and leans on it for stability. The beauty of this tow is the speed at which you can start towing, and the fact that you don't need specialized equipment to do it. If you find yourself having to tow a swimmer, the best way to do it is to have them climb up onto the stern of your boat and grab your waist or the cockpit coaming. They'll then press their chest hard against the deck to keep their center of gravity as low as possible, which makes the kayak more stable. This technique works so well because it keeps the swimmer out of the water, which makes the towing easiest and keeps the swimmer the warmest. Whatever tow you use, keep in mind that the conditions that made it necessary can often make it very dangerous, especially in rough seas or current where getting tangled in that line is a real concern. That's why you should practice all the different towing techniques in a controlled environment and only bring out the towline when it's really necessary." This is all accompanied by background music featuring a guitar.

audio_captions: Gentle, upbeat music plays. A man with a calm, clear voice says, "The Sage 17, designed by Jerry Montgomery exclusively for Sage Marine, is sized for adventure. If you want to go cruising with a group of friends,".
A man speaks, "sail into a crowded harbor under bluebird skies or...", accompanied by soft music.

Gentle guitar music plays as a narrator speaks, "haul 'em home with a reef in your main. The Sage 17 sets new standards for performance. That standard starts at the launch ramp with trailer options like an outboard motor mount for the auxiliary engine."

A male voice speaks, "14-inch tires with trailing arm torsion axles... and Sage uses a 35 lb lightweight mast with a simple stepping system that is easily handled by one person... There's even an integral tongue extension on the trailer. All these features are designed to get the boat in the water and you." This is accompanied by gentle acoustic guitar music.

A man speaks, "you're sailing with as little effort as possible. Because sailing is where the Sage 17 is truly sized for adventure. Whether you're setting off solo or sailing off the dock with a friend for an afternoon cruise." This is all accompanied by gentle background music featuring an acoustic guitar.
Background music plays as a male voice speaks, "The Sage 17's rigging is designed for easy performance under sail."
A person speaks, saying, "The headsail sheets, jib halyard, jib downhaul, and Cunningham all lead to the cabin top or cockpit."

Gentle, uplifting instrumental music plays in the background. A man speaks, "But performance is also about balance and control, and that starts with the Sage 17's 7/8ths rig. That comes standard with a backstay adjuster and a main sheet traveler with upwind sheeting. There's also an internal to the boom outhaul, a boom vang, internal to the mast halyards, and a Cunningham. These multiple controls allow the captain and crew to balance the rig for all sailing conditions, resulting in comfortable and efficient sailing. But it doesn't stop there. The Sage 17 can be ordered with roller furling or reefing headsails, multiple reef main, multiple hank-on headsails, tiller clutch by Wavefront, mainsail lugs with a mast gate. Each boat is built to order to meet her owner's sailing preferences, making the Sage 17 a perfect fit and the new standard for performance. The foundation for that performance is the classically styled lapstrake hull, which is both strong and dry. Here's what Howard Rice, adventurer and small boat expert, said in his product review of the Sage 17." A second man then speaks, "The 17 is a fine all-around pocket cruiser. Too often, designers pen boats that excel at only one or two aspects of sailing. I found the 17 to be an able performer across the board. She is both good-looking, fast, and remarkably stable, making her a compelling choice for near-shore coastal cruising. She offers ample room below for two plus lots of cruising gear. Her cabin is built of lightweight carbon fiber, thus eliminating the need for a mast support post. This feature gives her one large unobstructed double berth and lots of comfort. Given her 17-foot LOA, she is suited to purpose as a well-thought-out trailer cruiser for two. My wife and I had a marvelous cruise aboard the 17 and found her to be an excellent choice when selecting a trailer-able performance cruiser under 20 feet."

The woman says, "And you get some really nice..." The man says, "...what woman doesn't love a bit of sparkle, right, ladies?" A crackling sound is heard. The man says, "So here's a little magnesium along with... we can get some nice bright sparklies there, some white. You've seen those fireworks, right?" The woman replies, "I have, and I'm trying to take my chin up off the ground right now." The man says, "It's the magnesium. So do your iron again. A man speaks, "...magnesium and, you know, it it's the possibilities are endless." A woman then asks, "Well, I see that. A man speaks, "Testing circuit breakers is essential to ensure safe electricity supply, safe handling of network faults, and safety for the utilities personnel." A man speaks in a clear, measured voice, "and quickly became the world leader in this field. Ever since 2000, Omicron has been producing test equipment for substation commissioning and maintenance," accompanied by a soft, ambient electronic sound.

A man speaks in a clear, steady voice, "A major success factor for all of these devices has been their state-of-the-art power electronic design, making them multifunctional." This is accompanied by gentle, electronic background music.

A male voice speaks, "Omicron CIBANO 500, which combines all of the equipment that's needed for circuit breaker testing in one device," followed by a click. A low humming sound is present throughout.
A series of descending, synthesized musical notes.
A man speaks, "a micro-ohm meter, a multi-channel timing unit, a con..."

A person speaks, "controllable DC supply to power drive motors and trip and close coils. The integrated micro ohmmeter can measure contact resistance." This is followed by a mechanical clicking sound.
A male voice speaks, "while injecting up to 100 amps DC. The volt," accompanied by the sound of a low hum.
A male voice speaks, "is measured with a separate set of cables to determine the resistance." This is accompanied by a gentle electronic melody.

The male voice continues, "When measuring the opening and closing times of main and auxiliary contacts, as well as the deviations between them, the Subano can operate the trip and closing coils and automatically record the voltage and current signals in order to perform a comprehensive analysis." The audio ends with a loud, sharp bang.

A person says, "The CIBANO includes an integrated variable DC or AC voltage source that's used for generating the power for the tripping close coil operation or for supplying the drive motor," while electronic music plays.
A male voice speaks, "This is helpful during commissioning if the circuit breaker is in place, but the station battery isn't."

A person speaks: "What's more, this also helps to avoid wiring problems during hookup. Always applying the identical value of DC voltage makes measurements perfectly comparable." A clicking sound is then heard.

A man speaks, "Additionally, this allows a defined over or under voltage to be used to evaluate its impact on close and trip times. The output voltage of the Sabano's DC power supply is variable and can be used..." This is accompanied by a subtle electronic hum.

A man speaks, "perform the minimum pickup test and undervoltage trip test without changing the test connections." A click is heard, followed by a loud electrical buzz and a metallic clank. The voice continues, "Alternatively, the station DC supply can also be routed".
A person speaks, "through the Sibano to issue the trip and close commands. The coil currents and voltages are also recorded in this setup." This is followed by a low-pitched buzzing sound.
A man speaks, "With the Sabano 500, all of the typical circuit breaker tests can be performed efficiently and safely." This is followed by the sound of a switch clicking.
A low humming sound is followed by a bell-like chime.
A loud bang and a rattling sound, followed by a high-pitched beep.

audio_captions: Dramatic music plays in the background. A whooshing sound effect is heard as a male voice says, "Planet Dolan." A different, deeper-toned male voice speaks, "From killing thousands of people to end a war to choosing which of your children gets to live, we count eight of the hardest decisions people have had to make. Hey there, I'm Hellbent. I'm here to learn you suspiciously amazing facts that I didn't just make up."

A male voice speaks, "Number eight. In 2003, people all over the world let out a collective gasp after discovering the extreme lengths Aaron Ralston went to save his own life. Aaron had been canyoneering alone in Utah when he slid and became trapped under an". This is accompanied by a continuous, low-toned ambient score.

A male voice speaks, "enormous boulder. He survived for five days by drinking water and urine before losing all hope. After filming a goodbye message on his camera, Aaron made one of the hardest and most painful decisions anyone has ever had to make. For a slim chance at survival, he broke his own arm and amputated it using a miniature pair of pliers. This decision ultimately allowed him to escape and he..." A low, atmospheric musical drone is heard in the background.

A man speaks in a narrative tone, "survived against all odds. Nowadays, Aaron spends most of his time traveling around the world inspiring others as a motivational speaker. Number seven. A lawyer on Reddit shared the toughest moral dilemma of his entire career. He was defending a small company against a greedy corporation of scumbags. The case had huge stakes and losing it would cost his clients their livelihood. One day, while he's preparing for the case, the lawyer came across a very incriminating document. He knew that when the opposition found this document, they would spin it to win the case. All night he thought about destroying it to save his case. He wrestled with this for hours until it made him physically sick. In the end, he decided not to destroy it and was certain the bad guys would win. Sure enough, the opposition tried to use the document to incriminate the defendant. But against all odds, the jury saw through it. The truth came out and the defendant was proven innocent. The lawyer was so grateful he chose not to sell his soul and break the law, proving that some lawyers actually do have a soul. Number six. Some decisions are so tough they can shatter lifelong friendships. Childhood friends Henry and Pete have always had each other's back. So when Pete confessed he was having some serious financial problems, Henry didn't hesitate to bail him out. But Pete kept coming back asking for more and more money. Eventually, he admitted that he had a secret gambling problem and was in very hot water with some dangerous loan sharks. Henry thought long and hard about whether to bail his friend out again and eventually decided not to help him. He knew Pete would never turn his situation around unless he took responsibility and dealt with his addiction." This is all accompanied by somber background music.

A male narrator with a deep voice says, "Pete was furious and ended the friendship for many years, but after hitting rock bottom, he was finally able to sort his life out. It was hard for them to be out of each other's lives, but in the end, Pete said Henry's difficulties..."

A deep-voiced male speaker says, "decision, helped them find his way again. Their friendship is now stronger than ever." A different voice announces, "Number 5." The first speaker continues, "In 2010, Rachel Edwards made a choice that no parent should ever have to make. She decided which of her two children got to live. While they were on their way to see family, the car hit a pot hole. Rachel immediately lost control of the vehicle and they crashed into a levee. As water rushed in, Rachel had just seconds to choose which child to take to the surface. She..."

A male narrator speaks, "ultimately grabbed her two-year-old daughter Isabella and swam for the surface. Because of Isabella's age, it was impossible for Rachel to leave her and swim back down. So her six-" This is accompanied by dramatic background music.

Somber background music plays as a man with a deep voice speaks, "-year-old son Jack tragically drowned. Rachel is haunted by the fact that she couldn't save her son and wishes she could go back and somehow save both children. Her last memory of her son was him putting his hand out to protect her as the car began to sink. Number four. In 2010, a first-time mom's extreme pregnancy complications forced her to make the most painful decision ever. After some tests, her doctors told her things weren't looking right and that there was a strong chance she would bleed out without medical intervention. Her only options were to wait it out and see if things improved or terminate the pregnancy and save her own life. After years of trying to conceive, she made the heartbreaking decision to terminate her pregnancy and save her own life. The doctors told her to say her goodbyes, then gave her a shot of potassium chloride to stop her son's heart. She survived her operation and made a full recovery, but her son's sacrifice will weigh heavily on her for the rest of her life. Number three. In 1972, a plane crashed in the South American Andes. The only survivors were members and associates of the Uruguayan rugby team. To get enough food to stay alive, these people had to make one of the most haunting decisions ever. For months, they waited to be rescued in extremely grueling conditions, but with food supplies dwindling and radio reports notifying them that the search party had given up, the survivors became discouraged. They decided that the only way that they could stay alive long enough for someone to find them was if they fed on the dead bodies of their fellow passengers, many of whom were their friends. These corpses had been preserved in the snow and more became available when a further eight members of their group died in an avalanche. After a grueling two months, the final 16 survivors were rescued on the 23rd of December 1972. No doubt this experience changed them forever. Number two."

A dramatic piano score plays as a man speaks in a low, narrative voice: "In 2015, the Rong family was faced with an impossible choice. Their two sons had fallen suddenly ill and desperately needed kidney transplants to live. They took some test and determined that their father's high blood pressure made him ineligible as a donor. Luckily, their mother, Leon, was a suitable match, but with only one kidney to spare, she was forced to choose which of her sons would get to live. After many discussions and arguments, the eldest son decided that the kidney should go to his little brother, Li Hasong, who was studying to be a doctor. The operation took eight hours and ultimately was a success, but tragically, the family couldn't afford a second operation or get their hands on a second kidney. Number one. In August 1945, US President Harry Truman made one of history's most controversial decisions. In a desperate attempt to end World War II, he made the..."

A deep voice speaks, "executive call to drop atomic bombs over Hiroshima and Nagasaki. This devastated both cities and forced Japan to unconditionally surrender. Over 200,000 people lost their lives, and the few survivors suffered the long-lasting effects of radiation poisoning. People still debate about whether President Truman made the right decision." This is accompanied by somber background music.

A male character speaks in a deep voice, "Some believe America could have taken more humane actions to force Japan's surrender, while others insist this would have taken too long, cost too much, and potentially cost even more lives. However you feel, there's no denying that President Truman's difficult decision had huge repercussions and shaped the world today. And now for another question. What's the worst you've overreacted? Let us know on the Reddit page linked below and you might be featured in a future countdown. And that's all I got for now. Thanks for watching and I'll see you next time." This is accompanied by a low, sustained musical tone. Chiptune music plays, followed by a female character speaking, "Company's legal troubles began when Metallica found that a demo of their song, I Disappear, was circulating around the network. Radio stations had begun playing the song prior to the song's release. As you can imagine, this resulted in Metallica filing a lawsuit against Napster." A gentle musical score plays in the background.

A person says, "So we have here just a basic standard like vinyl leather jacket," while the sound of material rustling can be heard.
A female voice says, "And basically what I did was I took the EL wire."
A male voice asks, "What is EL wire?" A clinking sound is heard, followed by a female voice stating, "Electroluminescent wire."
A person speaks, "It's kind of got a bit of a flexibility to it. So if you, if you were to take it and wind it, it stays pretty well." This is followed by a short "Hmm" sound.

A female voice speaks, "And it just comes like this with a battery pack and whatnot, and you can have different settings. You can make it flash." A clicking sound is heard. The speaker continues, "all that. And what I did was I just figured out which seams I wanted the EL wire to go on. And I used transparent nylon thread, basically fishing line. It's really strong though, so it's it's better than fishing line in a sense that it's strong, but it's also thinner, so it's more like thread thread. And what I did was I just went around the EL wire along any of the seams that I wanted to show up, and voilà." The rustling of fabric can be heard.

A woman speaks, "And then I wound the EL wire around the outside edge so that it would stay on continuously because as a..." A ripping sound occurs. She continues, "...as a kid's toy, you know, you can turn it on and it'll go on and it'll make cool noises and whatnot, but it doesn't stay on. And then I just took Velcro..." Another ripping sound is heard. She finishes by saying, "...black Velcro, and sewed that to the back of the jacket."

A female voice says, "And then it stays on it." A male voice replies, "That just sounds exceedingly simple, like anybody could do that." The female voice continues, "I know, right? There you go. Instant cool rave gear. And if you're going to get really technical, you could do this in circuit board shapes and whatnot to create a more authentic Tron style suit." The male voice then says, "Oh, yeah."

A male speaker says, "I look like the Tron guy when I tried doing it. Do you guys see the Tron guy from..." A female speaker says, "That just means you need a Tron girdle. Is that what that means?" The male speaker says, "I I yeah, that's..." The female speaker laughs. The male speaker asks, "Do you guys remember the Tron guy?"

audio_captions: Dramatic and suspenseful orchestral music plays.
A swelling, dramatic musical score plays, and a male voice says, "On April 27th, the leaders of North and South Korea met for an historic summit."
A male voice says, "And it's only the third time that leaders of the two Koreas have met face to face. The summit comes after..." This is accompanied by gentle piano music.
A man says, "of ups and downs," accompanied by a ticking sound.
A male voice speaks, "North Korea conducted 20 ballistic missile tests and even tested a hydrogen bomb," accompanied by a tense musical underscore.
A man speaks, "But South Korea's Winter Olympics opened the door to dialogue, culminat..."
A male voice speaks, "in the summit at the DMZ." This is accompanied by subtle, dramatic background music.
A man speaks, "We hear from our top Korea experts on the implications of the meeting, the impact on relations." This is accompanied by background music.

A man speaks, "...nations with the United States, and whether this could be the final chapter in over three decades of brinkmanship." A woman then says, "North Korea's definition of denuclearization of the Korean peninsula or North Korea's concept of denuclearization of the Korean peninsula is different from that of the United States where we're just talking about North Korea giving up nuclear weapons. But I do think this is this sets a nice, it's a nice prelude to upcoming summit between President Trump and Kim Jong Un. President Moon knows they have to deliver something. South Koreans know they have to deliver something out of this Inter-Korean meeting to the United States to make sure that Trump Kim Jong Un's meeting go successfully. They will be one of the main goals for President Moon because President Moon knows no matter how successful Inter-Korean summit is, the climax really is Trump Kim meeting. And that has to go to be that has to be successful. So I think President Moon is going to try to really hard work hard to try to set that up." All of this is accompanied by subtle, electronic background music.

A man speaks, "There are three big lines of effort that come out of this summit. One is North-South dialogue. That's an important thing. There are dozens and dozens of North Koreans and South Koreans who have been separated, hundreds, by the Korean War who are in their 80s and 90s. On a humanitarian basis, it makes a lot of sense to try to give them an opportunity to meet their cousins, brothers, once again. The North needs humanitarian aid. If there's a way the South can help provide it, ensuring that it goes to the people who need it, not the army, that's worthwhile. Reducing tensions between the two Koreas is worthwhile. That line makes sense. The other two lines of effort being advertised are denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. Uh, anyone who's dealt with the North Koreans over the last 20, 25 years on this question, Republican or Democrat, will be deeply skeptical." A second man speaks, "It's hard for me to imagine that North Korea would agree to fully give up all of their nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles in a verifiable fashion without some attenuation of the US alliance commitment to South Korea, because for the North, that would mean the end of US hostile policy towards North Korea. But the United States security commitment to South Korea is 60 years old. It is one of our core positions in Asia. And so it's very difficult for me to imagine that the United States would attenuate that commitment." The first man continues, "North Korea in 2012 declared that it is a nuclear weapon state. It's not going to change that. It might, might give access to, maybe even destroy some element of its nuclear weapons program, perhaps associated with the Yongbyon reactor, which is now three decades old and not very useful. But the diplomacy with North Korea has always been stopped by the question of verification. How do you verify that North Korea is in fact giving up its nuclear weapons? They've never granted, uh, meaningful verification opportunities that they are dismantling in an irreversible way their programs. Uh, there's no evidence that this summit or the follow-on summits with Donald Trump and others will yield that in any meaningful well. So that's a big question mark."

Soft, ambient music plays in the background as a woman speaks, saying, "I think for China, China welcomes this development, and China will welcome a Trump-Kim Jong-un meeting, particularly if it leads to some sort of a deal, either freeze-for-freeze or even reduction of US troops from South Korea. All of that works for China. For Japan, I think their view of this summit is mixed. On one hand, it does signify a step towards a more peaceful end, or it's at least a step away from all this potential conflict taking place in the Korean peninsula. So that must be a relief. On the other hand, this sets up a meeting between Kim, Kim Jong-un and President Trump, and Japan is a little bit worried about a potential deal that could be made between Washington and Pyongyang because they don't want a deal that just involves intercontinental ballistic missile or even freeze-for-freeze or even peace treaty, because that doesn't really help Japan and Japan's security concerns."
Gentle, melodic music is playing.

A man speaks, "The first thing is that we have to remember that a summit is not a strategy, and a summit without a strategy is dangerous, right? If the summit fails, then there's nowhere else to go, because we're at the end of diplomacy, right? So, we have to remember that the other side of a summit is a cliff. And if these summits are not carefully prepared and negotiated in advance, their failure could actually increase the chances for war. The only conceivable way that I could see the North Koreans giving up their weapons is if the United States ended its security commitment to South Korea or guaranteed the security of the entire Korean peninsula. And I don't see either of those things as being possible at the moment."

A man speaks, "The North Koreans went into this with no intention of giving up their nuclear weapons. When Pyongyang uses phrases like denuclearization of the Korean peninsula, history, including my own experience negotiating with the North Koreans, demonstrates very clearly what they mean is, after the US ends its nuclear umbrella, stops sanctioning North Korea, stops what North Korea calls its hostile policy, then and only then will North Korea consider itself giving up nuclear weapons. Anyone who's negotiated with the North Koreans in the past 20 years knows that that phrase sounds very tempting, but when North Korea says it's prepared for denuclearization of the Korean peninsula, it's actually quite meaningless." Another man begins to speak, "What price is the United States willing to pay for denuclearization? Has that price gone up from the past to agreements that we have made? Um, what price are we willing to accept for failure of the negotiation? Are we willing to accept the higher cost of war that could come with a failure of the negotiation? In the end, the success of any negotiation will depend on whether the United States or North Korea is willing to change or compromise their core position, because these core positions are diametrically opposed to one another." The first man resumes speaking, "All eyes will be on Donald Trump. He himself wants a big, dramatic, history-making summit with Kim Jong Un. That's a bit dangerous if you're Japan or if you're the Pentagon. On the other hand, his national security team, many of them, people like National Security Advisor John Bolton, Secretary of Defense Mattis, his Assistant Secretary for Asia, Randy Schriver, they know all of these pitfalls, traps, risks associated with charging pell-mell into a peace agreement that is actually no peace agreement at all, but possibly and very dangerously, a post-facto legitimization of North Korea's nuclear weapons. That's a very, very slippery and dangerous slope. So, the debates within the administration and with Congress will now intensify. The fact we're talking is good, but we haven't seen the North Korean nuclear threat go away and the meeting we've had gives no indication that it will go away. So the problem's not solved and there will be a lot of scrutiny that's necessary as we go through the next chapter in this increasingly dramatic, hopeful but not risk-free part of the Korean Peninsula denuclearization and diplomatic process." A third man with a deeper voice says, "For more analysis on the future of the Korean peninsula, visit the Korea Chair on CSIS.org or visit Beyond Parallel."

audio_captions: A gentle acoustic guitar melody plays as a woman with a clear and friendly voice speaks, "Hi, I'm Angela from High Quality Organics, one of the largest suppliers of organic herbs, spices, teas, and blends. And today, I'd like to share some insight on one of the largest health concerns facing Americans today, sodium. According to the Center for Disease Control, over 90% of Americans are consuming too much sodium. In fact, even children are at risk for excess sodium consumption."

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "Why is eating too much salt such a big deal? Well, excess sodium consumption puts us at risk for high blood pressure, which is often a precursor to heart disease, the leading cause of death in the US. It also puts us at risk for stroke." This is accompanied by the sound of an acoustic guitar playing a gentle melody.
A gentle acoustic guitar melody plays.

A woman speaks in a clear, informative tone, "So where is all this excess salt coming from? I'm sure most of you already know the answer to that question. Packaged foods. 65% of the salt that we consume in our diets comes from packaged foods. Only 25% comes from the foods we enjoy at restaurants, and a mere 5% from the salt we add to our food at the dinner table." This is all accompanied by soft, instrumental music.
A gentle, melodic piece of music is played on an acoustic guitar.

A woman speaks in a clear, presentational tone: "While many manufacturers are working very hard to reduce sodium from their food formulations, they're learning that a reduced sodium claim often hinders sales. In fact, Mentel, a well-known market research firm, has discovered that there's been a 5% reduction in reduced sodium claims from 2010 to 2011. The fact is, salt enhances flavor, and when consumers see a reduced sodium claim on a food package, they automatically assume that that food probably lacks flavor. Several years ago, High Quality Organics developed an all-purpose no salt blend, and our aim was simple. We wanted to help food companies reduce sodium without losing flavor. Our all-purpose no salt blend is a beautiful combination of herbs with a slightly spicy finish. It's great for vegetable dishes or really any dish. Because our all-purpose no salt blend has been so popular, we've developed several others. Our no salt barbecue blend, perfect for a rub on a dark meat or your favorite chicken. It has a great balance of salt and sweet and it has a hint of onion and garlic. And for all you garlic lovers out there, we have a no salt garlic blend. It's a wonderful blend of citrus herbs and garlic and it's great for chicken, vegetables, or fish dishes. Now, if you're not crazy about garlic, but you love seafood, our no salt seafood blend might be the one for you. It has a wonderful combination of citrus and herbs and it's great for any fish. And for those of you who like a little kick to your dish, we have our no salt spicy blend. It marries wonderfully with soups, stews, or slow cooker meals." Throughout the speech, the sound of a small glass jar being placed on a hard surface is heard several times.

A woman speaks, "These products speak for themselves. They continue to be our number one selling group of blends at High Quality Organics. If you'd like to learn more information or order, please visit our website at www.hqorganics.com. We're also on Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and Pinterest. So please stop by and say hi." This is accompanied by gentle acoustic guitar music.

audio_captions: Flowing electronic music plays, followed by a woman speaking in a clear voice, "Gelatin zymography. Zymography is a simple, sensitive, quantifiable, and functional assay for the analysis of enzyme activity in tissue or in polyacrylamide gel. There are many variations of the technique. We will demonstrate here gelatinase activity assay by SDS-PAGE, taking conditioned medium from animal cell culture as source of gelatinase activity. Principle." The music continues quietly in the background throughout the speech.

Soft instrumental music plays in the background. A woman speaks in a clear voice, "In conditioned media of mammalian cells contain matrix metalloproteinases, MMP2 and MMP9. They are released from cells in a proteolytically inactive proform, called a zymogen. Because the inactive form becomes activated during the process of denaturation and renaturation after gel electrophoresis, the active form of the enzyme degrade the substrate gelatin. After the electrophoretic run, the SDS is soaked out from the gel at a zymogram by incubation in Triton X-100, a detergent, followed by incubation in an appropriate buffer for an optimized length of time and temperature. The gelatin hydrolyzed zones are seen as white bands against blue background of the gel when it is stained with Coomassie brilliant blue."
A calm female voice says, "procedure," accompanied by gentle music.

A female voice speaks, "Assemble the glass plate on a clean surface. Lay the longer glass plate down first and then place a shorter glass plate on top of it. Embed them into the casting frame and clamp them properly. Make sure that the bottom ends of the glass plates are properly aligned. Place the casting frame onto the casting stand. Pour some distilled water between the arranged glass plates to check the leaking between the plates. Remove the water by placing a blotting paper in between the glass plate as shown. Place a comb in between the glass plates and make a mark 1 cm below the comb teeth. Take a blue capped tube and label it as resolving gel." This is accompanied by soft instrumental background music.

A female voice with a neutral tone speaks, "Preparation of 10% resolving gel. The reagents used are: 5 ml of gelatin solution made in 1.5 molar Tris of pH 8.8, 30% acrylamide bis-acrylamide mixture of 3.5 ml, 82.5 microliter of 10% SDS, 82.5 microliters of 50% glycerol, ammonium persulfate or APS of 100 microliter, and 0.010 ml or 10 microliter of TEMED which should be kept in an ice box. Once the TEMED is added to the mix, immediately pour the resolving gel into the glass plate up to the mark drawn. Pour 1 ml of water-saturated butanol above the resolving gel layer. Allow the gel to polymerize for 20 to 30 minutes. During this time, prepare the stacking gel." This is accompanied by gentle background music.

Soft, instrumental music plays in the background as a woman speaks: "The composition of 5% stacking gel. 3.4 ml of distilled water. 0.83 ml of 30% acrylamide, bis-acrylamide mix. 0.63 ml of one molar Tris of pH 6.8. 0.05 ml of 10% SDS. Add these reagents into a blue capped tube labeled stacking gel. After the gel has polymerized, water saturated n-butanol layer was absorbed by placing a blotting paper in between the glass plates. Now add 0.05 ml of APS and 0.005 ml of TEMED from the ice box to the blue capped tube. Immediately pour the stacking gel in between the glass plates till it overflows. Now place a comb in the stacking gel sandwich and allow the gel to polymerize for 10 minutes. Meanwhile, prepare the samples for loading into the wells of the gel. Mix the protein samples with 4X gel loading dye in the ratio 4:1."
A female voice says, "to run the gel."

A female speaker with a clear voice says, "Take out the apparatus from the casting frame and clamp it onto the gel apparatus. Make sure the short plate always faces inside and if you have only one plate to run, keep a dummy plate for balance. Keep the plates in the cassette and then lock it. Now place this cassette in the tank. Fill the inner chamber of the tank with 1x running buffer of pH 8.3. Now remove the comb carefully without breaking the wells. Rinse the wells with 1x running buffer using syringe. Rinse a loading tip with buffer. Samples can now be loaded onto the gel. Deliver the 20 microliters of the protein sample into the well. Carefully, by inserting the tip to a few millimeters from the well bottom without breaking the wells. Rinse the loading tip with the buffer after each loading. Close the lid of the gel tank and connect the wires to electrical circuit. Make sure the connection is proper, that is black lead to black and red lead to red. Now set the voltage at 150 volt and run for about one hour or until the dye front runs to the end of the gel. Now switch off the power supply and disconnect the electrical leads. Take out the gel plates and remove the gel from the plates into a box. Wash the gel with distilled water. Pour Triton X-100 into the box containing gel and keep it for five minutes in the orbit shaker. Repeat this step thrice. Discard the Triton X-100 solution and add low salt collagenase buffer into the gel and leave overnight on an orbit shaker or minimum for four to six hours. After overnight incubation, discard the low salt collagenase buffer and pour staining solution into the gel. Keep it for 30 minute incubation in orbit shaker. Destain the gel until the bands are properly seen. The presence of gelatinolytic activity of protein samples loaded will be seen as clear bands against a blue background." This is accompanied by gentle instrumental background music.

audio_captions: Rhythmic, upbeat music plays. An announcer says, "Welcome to the one-minute apologist. We interview the world's leading apologists to provide credible answers to curious questions." A man speaks, "So, I know that outside of being a detective, you served for some time as a pastor as well. You've had a unique look as a lay person and as ministry and now as a Christian apologist to really be able to see the church from different angles. What kind of advice would you give to pastors for equipping their church in this melting pot culture of beliefs so that we can see less people making a mass exodus from the church?"

Light, rhythmic background music plays as a male speaker says, "Yeah, I think it's a challenge. And first of all, I have a heart for pastors because I think what they face is is really an incredible task and and I can't even know one human that could do even do this job anymore, I don't know. But but I can tell you that I think it's it's important for pastors to realize there's two prongs you've got to prepare your people for."

A male speaker says, "One, is our our our our congregations prepared to make a case against a world that doesn't even accept any of our claims? The other problem of course is internal." This is accompanied by background music.

A man speaks over a low, ambient musical tone, saying, "is do we even know enough about what our system teaches, about what our system claims? Do we have enough systematic theology to be able to withstand error that's in the church?"

A person speaks in a clear voice, "So you've got two fronts. One, the outside world is pressing against us, and the inside turmoil we sometimes see with people who hold errant views. So, I think you have two, two prongs there."
A man speaks, "But I recently, it was interesting. I recently did a a conference at a church that gave an entire month every summer to an apologetics five-week series or four-week series."
A man speaks: "And I thought, what, my gosh, think about it. Getting a four or four weeks out of 52 to apologetics. I think in the end all of us as church leaders..."

A man speaks in a clear, measured tone, "are going to have to decide what percentage of Christian casemaking it should warrant in our calendars each year. And we can talk a lot about wanting to change the course of our church." This is accompanied by a soft, ambient musical track.

A person speaks, "...or wanting to get our our people all of our changes have to begin with a calendar. We got to say to ourselves, okay, so if this is important to us," This is accompanied by background music and rhythmic clicks.

A person speaks, "You know if I want to know about you and what's important to you, I need to look at your checkbook and your calendar. Because what you do and what you spend your money on are probably what you're you're passionate about." This is accompanied by background music.
A person speaks, "And as a church too, I think we need to do the same thing. What are we spending our time on and then what are we giving our money to?" This is accompanied by background music.

A man speaks in a conversational tone, "That'll tell us a lot about who we are as a people. So I think my my encouragement for pastors is, I know it's a big and tough job." This is accompanied by soft background music.
A male voice speaks clearly, "But at some point we're probably all going to have to make a decision about what percentage of our church life we're going to give over to the defense of the gospel."

A person speaks, "but preparing our people to make the case for Christ. And I think that's really the challenge we all have. I think I think we just kind of just stand tall to that challenge and embrace it rather than hand it off to somebody else." This is accompanied by subtle background music.
A man says, "Again, we write books on apologetics. I would love for pastors to become the books on apologetics for their congregations." This is followed by a rhythmic, synthesized music track.

audio_captions: Indistinct chatter and music can be heard in the background as a male voice speaks, "We are at DevCon 2010 taking a look at Research in Motion's new Blackberry Playbook. We cannot touch this display unit but we can get a close-up look at it. The display, once it comes back on, as you can see, is absolutely fantastic. It's a really, really beautiful display. Even from behind the glass, you can tell the quality is just there. Very bright, very nice to look at."
A male voice speaks, "on the BlackBerry PlayBook, we've got two," followed by a short electronic beep.

A man speaks, "cutouts. One is a camera, another is a light sensor. Down at the bottom, we have a USB connector. And here's a look at the display. We can't really, like I said, go around and touch it, but what we can tell is that it is extremely thin. It's really nice to see this device that'll be very, very mobile. It's not quite small enough to shove in a pocket, but it should slip in and out of a bag or a purse very easily. On the back, we have the Blackberry logo. We also have an indicator of the capacity. This model is a 32-gigabyte model. Over to in the other display, we have a 16-gigabyte model. Up top, you can see that there is just a few buttons. We've got a power switch, volume controls, and a play-pause function button." All of this is accompanied by upbeat electronic music and faint background chatter.

A person speaks, "down below. you can see that this is a small USB connector, um and there appears to be a couple other slots there, we're not sure exactly what that is, it may be a speaker output. One thing that's interesting is over here in this display model, this is a new".

A man speaks, "functioning mock-up prototype. You can see that this back is blue. So hopefully BlackBerry will let their users choose a color that fits their lifestyle best. Another interesting thing here is that in this BlackBerry PlayBook demo room is there's a bunch of posters up around the walls. And while this is clearly a device geared towards business people, there's only one poster that has anything to do with business and that's this poster about BlackBerry PlayBook's email client. If you look over to the other posters, we've got one showing off a photo album and a camera roll. We've got". This is all accompanied by the sound of background chatter.

A man speaks, "another you're showing a video playing demonstration of a video playing a uh looks like a piano concert or music video of some kind. And over here we have an audio uh media player. So while this is a business device, BlackBerry and Research in Motion are known as a business mobile device makers. They are trying to appeal to consumers, because after all, just about every consumer is a business person, has a day job as well as uh loves enjoying media at nighttime."

audio_captions: A male narrator speaks, "Back in San Jose, she's come so close but for Ashley Wagner, it's never been quite her time. After another disappointing season, she moved cross country to train with legendary coach John Nicks, hoping he might have the answers she needed." This is followed by a gentle musical chime, and then a female voice says, "She is one of the..."
A male voice says, "few young ladies that I've told that has..."

Soft, gentle music plays in the background as a person speaks, "Great combination of athleticism and artistry. What I saw was a skater that had a multitude of talents that really hadn't ever achieved her potential."
A male voice says, "at times I felt she also became".
A man speaks, "very focused and under pressure certainly at nationals. Perhaps the training".
A male voice speaks, "wasn't as disciplined mentally as it should have been." This is followed by a female voice saying, "The past couple of C's."
A female voice speaks, "I felt like I was just the almost girl. I was tired of almost being, you know, national champion," accompanied by the sound of a soft piano melody.
A female voice says, "almost getting top two, almost making the world team, almost making the Olympic team."
A female voice says, "Almost, almost, almost so close that, you know, I could just almost touch it." A different female voice then says, "Mr. Nix is by far unlike any."
A person says, "coach that I've ever".

A woman's voice says, "with the floor. He is very set in his ways." A man's voice follows, "I think Ashley's a lot more confident in performance now than she was when she came to me." Another woman then states, "Mentally, this is my nationals to lose." This is all set against a backdrop of emotional music.
A female voice speaks, "I'm the one who is going to be holding myself back," accompanied by background music.

A woman speaks, "I'm the one who's going to mess it up if anything. That's what I'm going to have to overcome." A male commentator says, "So Ashley, now a California girl with a new coach, new programs, and a new attitude." Another man announces, "Now the final skater in group three of the championship ladies short program, representing the Skating Club of Wilmington, it's 20-year-old Ashley Wagner." A woman says, "She's got it all. She just has to let it happen, not make it happen." Classical music begins to play, accompanied by the sound of ice skates gliding. A female commentator speaks over the music, "It's just a different kind of calmness to her skating and a joy that I have not seen. And it's usually the short program where she has her problems."

Orchestral music plays. A male speaker says, "She needs to get past this next pass here. Triple loop." The music continues, accompanied by the sound of skates on ice. A female speaker then says, "It's not very many competitors who announce that they're going to win a competition. It's certainly not common to hear in figure skating."
A male voice says, "He said these Nationals are mine to lose." Orchestral music plays, followed by the roar of a crowd.

A crowd cheers and applauds. A male announcer speaks, "The fist pump says that is the new and improved Ashley Wagner." The crowd continues to cheer and applaud as a male announcer says, "And the score puts her in third place. 63.06 after the short program." A voice over a public address system says, "She's currently in third place." A female voice says, "Hey everyone. The curse of the short program is finally broken. Thanks so much to my team and me actually keeping my head on straight. Tonight going in, practices have been going really well. I was feeling confident, but I got out onto the ice and it kind of all hit me at once that it was Nationals and it was the short program and I had some demons to overcome. So I am so proud of myself and the fact that I did it." Dramatic orchestral music plays, followed by a male announcer's voice saying, "Welcome back once again to beautiful San Jose, California. Continuing coverage of the..."

A male announcer says, "2012 Prudential US Figure Skating Championships." Over the sound of applause, a female announcer says, "Ashley Wagner. She has amongst all the women the most, the deepest file..."

A woman speaks over the sound of a cheering crowd, saying, "burning in her belly right now. She has had three very difficult seasons. She's back. She skated a clean short program, usually her nemesis. And she is focused and fit and ready." Upbeat, dramatic music begins as a man says, "The final group, six skaters coming up to decide the US Ladies Championship." Another man then says, "somebody who skated with a lot of confidence in that short program. It's Ashley Wagner," as crowd noise is heard.

The sound of ice skates is heard as a man speaks, "...in third place after that short program. Felt that she killed her short program demon." Another man says, "Ashley Wagner in striking position in third place." A third man speaks over background music, "Ashley version three. You know, every time we see her, it's she's sort of, you know, transformed. And this time, this is the most calm, this is the most relaxed, and this is the most..." A woman interjects, "Joyous." The man continues, "...joyous. Absolutely in the short program. It's fun to watch." The crowd cheers and applauds as a man says, "So Ashley Wagner put the demons of..."

An audience applauds, followed by a man speaking, "put her short program behind her with her performance on Thursday night. Moved cross country to train with John Nicks. She's now a California girl. A new attitude, new programs, can she do it?" This is accompanied by the sound of ice skating. Music then begins to play.
Orchestral music plays, accompanied by the sound of ice skates scraping on ice. A man says, "Now the most difficult jump in this program."
Majestic, orchestral music plays, and a soft voice says, "Beautiful."

Orchestral music plays. A man speaks energetically, "Incredibly difficult entrance that triple loop, beautifully landed," as a crowd cheers. A woman says, "And she's confident," followed by, "I mean, she's delivering." The sound of ice skating can be heard.

A person speaks, "And here she's ready to paint. I always use a long list for focus." Cheering and applause from a crowd can be heard, accompanied by orchestral music. A man says, "Amazing what a change of scenery can do." A woman laughs and responds, "It is." The crowd continues to cheer and applaud.

The sound of applause is heard. An announcer says, "Ashley Wagner," followed by more applause. Another announcer with a deep voice speaks over cheering, "Her score for the free skate, 123.96." A commentator replies, "That's a monster score." The announcer continues, "Total score, 187.02. She is currently in first place." A commentator says, "Oh, both personal bests for Ashley Wagner. 123.96 for the free skate and a 187.02 for the competition." Another commentator speaks over continued cheering, "And so Ashley Wagner, no longer the almost girl, she's now the golden girl." A woman laughs. The commentator adds, "She's waited a long time for this. And it wasn't her lack of work or effort that kept her from that title, it was just minor accidents."

A male speaker says, "And let's go to Andrea Joyce in the AT&T athlete lounge." A female speaker responds, "Tom, we've been talking about it all night. Ashley, you said you were tired of being the almost girl. What is it like to be the 'it' girl finally?" Another female speaker replies, "It has been years since I've been on the top of any podium, let alone nationals. I'm, I'm in shock. I am so extremely happy. I don't even know..." All of this is accompanied by the sound of a crowd cheering.

A person speaks with an emotional, shaky voice, "what to say. I just I've worked so hard and I've sacrificed so much this year and for it to finally pay off and to have some results to show for it. I'm I'm ecstatic."

audio_captions: Dramatic and suspenseful orchestral music plays.

A woman speaks, "stuck at number three, why should they be number one?" A man then replies, "Well, I think you've hit on a couple of points. First of all,"

A man speaks, "Florida State is two and oh against top 25 teams. Alabama is just one and one. I think everyone talks about this eye test. I think you guys are missing, those of you out there who think Florida State should be number three. Part of an eye test is looking around a football field, look up at the scoreboard, because Florida State is 10 and oh. No one else can say there are zero losses on their record. I mean, think about what the committee is proposing and what I suppose anyone is proposing to think the Seminoles should be third. In the history of college football, a team from a power conference, undefeated, being left out of what would be the national championship game. I mean, imagine last year Florida State gets left out because two one-loss teams like like Auburn or Michigan State play each other for the national title game. It's illogical, there's no precedents for this. Makes no sense for Florida State to not be on top right now." A rhythmic beat plays in the background during part of his speech. A woman then says, "Brian, thank you. Jeff, hang tight because I want to ask you one more."

A person speaks, "specific question. I think the challenge in a lot of people's minds with Florida State is that besides falling behind early in so many games that the ACC quite frankly isn't chock full of strong opponents. People wonder if FSU would be able to rally against an Ole Miss defense, an Alabama defense, a Wisconsin defense. As somebody who watches that team as closely as you do, how do you think they'd fare against better defenses?"

A man speaks in a conversational tone: "Well, I think we start with this premise, this assumption that this SEC is so phenomenal. I think we're taking that based on history. And the reason history shows me there's a team that's won 26 in a row. SEC, I don't know that they've proven themselves on the field the way we think that they have in the past. I mean this"

A male speaker says, "'Bama, Mississippi State, Ole Miss. If I'm not mistaken, combined out of conference, they've played one Power Five team. They just haven't shown it to the country. They keep..." This is accompanied by a rhythmic electronic beat.

A man speaks, "beating up themselves, which is great, but you're not proving you're what you say you are. I mean, even the Pac-12 South has more teams in the top 25 than the SEC West. audio_captions: A man speaks, "Lonzo Ball responding to the haters after his lackluster first game in this second game. He dropped a triple-double. 11 points, 11 rebounds, 11 assists. There goes one of them. And he's going up against Jayson Tatum. Tatum with a monster game, 27 points, 11 rebounds on 9 of 19 shooting. And he was doing it in the post. Look at these fadeaways. He's looking like Dirk in his prime, one-legged. Check out that replay. Making it look easy. But first, let's talk about Lonzo. The best thing about his rebounding is that he's the point guard, so when he gets one, he can start the fast break immediately. Loves to push the pace. And he got a lot of assists that way in transition. Now one thing that I'm noticing from Lonzo, he's kind of like Ricky Rubio. He's predetermining his passes. So when he crosses somebody over, before he even gets in the lane, he just dishes it off. It's like he's telling himself, okay, on this possession I'm going to pass, on this possession I'm going to do a layup. And that was a nice move from Lonzo. And if you watch this entire game, then you know what I'm talking about because Lonzo would make the pass before the defense even collapses. He wasn't slashing to score, he was slashing to pass, like Rubio. He was passing up on layups to try to get the assist. And in the Summer League, when you're looking at some of these plays and you can rewind it and watch again, these defenders in the paint, they have no idea what they're doing. A lot of them are looking silly, they're way out of position with hands-up defense, they're throwing in the towel. But this problem for Lonzo can easily be fixed. As he gets more experience, as he gets more confidence, then he'll start attacking and making the decision based on what the defense does instead of predetermining, okay, I'm going to do a layup this time or I'm going to pass this time. I don't think Magic Johnson is going to let him develop that bad habit that Ricky Rubio has. I think he's going to snap him out of it. Make him more dynamic and dangerous. And in this game, Lonzo's shot selection was not terrible like it was in the first game. He didn't chuck up 11 threes. He took five threes, he only made one, but that's not that bad. They were good looks." This is all accompanied by upbeat background music.

A male voice speaks against a backdrop of music, "He wasn't forcing the shot like last game, shooting one of 11. Now we got to talk about Tatum, and you're seeing these highlights. He is a dynamic scorer. He's got so many post moves. He's scoring in so many different ways. He just looks like he's ready to go. I mean, he had 27 points in this game. Those are numbers that guys like LeBron and Wade and Kobe were dropping in the Summer League. So the Celtics definitely made the right decision by drafting him, by trading down, getting some..."

A character speaks, "more assets because he looks like he's going to work out. But it is a little bit weird though because they just signed Hayward. And Tatum looks like he's going to be a beast. So I guess until Tatum fully develops, they rock with Hayward and when Tatum's there, I think Tatum might end up being better than Hayward. It looks like his ceiling is higher. It could be higher. You never know, but that's the good thing about watching these rookies. You never know what's going to happen. A lot of the players today that are stars, if you look at the criticism that they got before they were a star, like somebody like Steph Curry, when he won his first championship, they started showing the ads of what people were saying before he made it to where he is now. And there goes Lonzo getting a triple double he's padding..." This is accompanied by background music.
A male voice says, "the stats a little bit. Let me know in the comments."

Electronic music plays as a person asks, "section, which player had more impact in this game? Was it Tatum with the 27 and 11 or Ball with the 11, 11 and 11?" Another person says, "Hippo. A man speaks, saying, "Teaching as research, in my mind has two elements. One, I think should be very easy for anybody who's participating in CIRTL, and that is just caring about how we teach and working to improve our teaching and helping our students. That, I think again, is a given for anybody involved in CIRTL, but the second part is a little trickier, and that's learning how to collect data on our teaching, to make sure that what we think is working is actually working. For example, I know one of my fellow instructors tried a new method of teaching something in one of our classes. And in our instructor meeting, we got together and she talked about how well it worked and how it was very easy to do, easy to implement, and the students really enjoyed it. And those are good outcomes. However, student enjoyment might not be the best criteria to use. So we need to be able to..."
A person speaks, "collect uh some sort of data to see".
A male voice speaks, "the students actually benefit from it. Did they really learn?"
A man speaks, "and that may be uh follow-up measures or measures after the fact to see if they retain the information that we wanted them to retain."
A person speaks, "I think that before I started fast, I really didn't know anything about teaching as research."

A woman speaks in a clear, measured tone: "And after going through the FAST program through CIRTL and doing a teaching as research project myself, what I really came to value was that teaching as research is a way that we can incorporate research questions into our teaching, into our classrooms. And so that sort of insatiable curiosity that we have as scientists, we can bring that to our classrooms. And we can ask questions about how students are learning, we can come up with hypotheses, we can test them, and we could do formal assessments. And um that could be valuable either to share with others as we're sharing our methods or just for ourselves. Teaching as research can be informal. We don't need to be um really formally assessing and communicating our results, but we can do it just as an informative assessment in our own classrooms to improve our teaching and improve the experience of the students."

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "To me, it's a really great way to become more engaged sort of in your teaching. So I've always known that education and teaching was going to be very important for me. It's kind of where I wanted my future career to go. But as far as having this idea that you can use what you're doing in your classroom, have a structure in place that will allow you to evaluate your teaching effectiveness and then hopefully inform not only what you'll do in the classroom in the future, but maybe some other people as well."

A person speaks in a clear voice, "um teaching as research really is more than what the words imply. It actually became more of a new language that I learned and the best part of teaching as research for me was being able to use this new language to communicate with uh".
A woman speaks, "teaching fellows, faculty, and researchers in other disciplines around this teaching and learning, uh, community."

A person speaks, "To me, teaching as research is implementing the same ideas that we borrow from the scientific method in the classroom. So it's coming up with a hypothesis that is addressing a real problem, so not, to me it's addressing something that you're actually seeing in your classroom, just not an idea that you think is neat, but rather something that will actually have an impact in your classroom. Then coming up with some sort of methodology that is supported in the literature to address that idea and then..."

A woman speaks, "coming up with specific goals and outcomes, just like you would in an experiment. Your experiments have specific objectives. So it's the same idea. Then coming up with tests that will evaluate that within again the framework of those goals and that hypothesis."

And so I was incorporating how to learn in not only my TAR project, but my discipline, research, and then, you know, any courses or anything, you know, just regular learning that occurs as a graduate student. Um, so those were...

A man speaks in a clear voice, "because that process I described is it's called the scientific method in the discipline research and it's exactly the same process that I take into my teaching as research."
A person speaks, "project of asking a question."
A person speaks, "deciding what will be accepted as".
A person speaks, "evidence um for the question. Um but it's also important in teaching and I found it challenging it it challenges your teaching because you're not just doing something and not".

A man speaks in a calm, measured voice, "collecting anything back. When you take the research mentality to the classroom, you're then looking for evidence and deciding, um, what you will select as evidence is whether learning took place. So for me, teaching as research is a philosophy that I integrate into my TAR project, um, my thesis research, and my teaching as well." A woman then speaks in a clear voice, "Well, I I'll say that um, we're still trying to kind of define exactly what it is. Um, but it's it really is inquiry-based teaching and and developing a hypothesis, asking a question, gathering data that can support that hypothesis or debunk that hypothesis and doing the analysis to figure out whether it was true or not true. And then hopefully the next step is what do you do based on that? You know, you got the results, how do you change your teaching and learning so that you become more effective? So, I would say it's it's very different than a TA-ship. It's"
A person speaks, "not going into the class and designing the curriculum and teaching the content and."

A person speaks, "interacting on a regular basis with the students. It's more about a well-defined question that you want to ask and that you want to gather data on and get an answer to. And so that was our biggest problem again getting back to the scope."
A person speaks, "that you can't solve how do students best learn math. It's just not possible. You have to have a well-defined question that you're going to answer."

A person speaks, "I would agree with that and I think it's also a really great way to get the students to dig into the literature and see that there is literature supporting good and effective teaching and that they can build on that the way you might build on your disciplinary literature and the research that's out there. Um, and I was also gonna add that for our students, one of the things that really helps um them take those disciplinary research skills and apply it in this context is having a question about what works. So, if you're going to address student misunderstanding about some part of the some content topic or something like that, thinking about a teaching approach and how it works in the context of that topic. So you're not answering those big questions in terms of the research around teaching and learning, but you're building on it and looking in the context of this particular course, does this approach work? And those seem to be really um effective ways of engaging students." Another person responds, "I've grown to see that teaching as research is a critical component of teaching. That we have to write learning outcomes and we have to create assessments and choose instruction and we should be studying all the time what students are doing in the class, how well is the is the learning happening. And so I'd like to see and I'd like to promote to our students that they should be thinking about this question all the time. And when they design the course, months before the course actually happens, they should be thinking, 'What could I do and build this teaching as research right into my course?' Instead of it being a an add-on that I did at the end because I accidentally had some test data that I could look at now. No, I want them to create homework assignments and and essay questions where the answers that they're going to grade and give feedback to the students and the data is there for them to investigate their research. That's the kind of teaching as research I'd like to see. If it blossomed into a more formal study that they could end up publishing or sharing at a conference, that's that would be..."

"a double bunce." A sound of agreement is heard, followed by a person speaking, "I think teaching's research projects are a really nice way to give them an opportunity to do that maybe in a more limited scope if they don't have the opportunity to be an instructor of record. A woman speaks: "teach. Right. And I think it's just like any other skill, the more you practice it, the more innate it becomes. You have to think ahead of time, how do you design your questions, what questions do you ask to"

A person speaks, "make sure that students are learning what it is you think they're learning. So, I mean from my perspective, the benefit of having graduate students and postdocs do this is it's going to become part of their nature. Whereas for faculty, this is a sort of foreign concept, and many faculty unfortunately don't approach their teaching this way."

A man speaks, "and our our students have had years of school doing experiment after experiment getting larger and larger and and more control over their design and then the analysis. So when they finally get to grad school or postdocs, they're doing big research projects in their labs that they're going to end up publishing. Another man replies, "Well, I think doing these projects in the context of CIRTL is really nice because it gives you a safe space to try. audio_captions: A person speaks, "Allergies turn your own body against you over something stupid."
A character speaks, "like strawberries."
A man speaks, saying, "We've got to be able to stop that."

Upbeat electronic music plays, followed by a man speaking, "Anthony here for DNews and allergies suck. There is no more annoying reminder of how fragile the human body really is than getting laid up in bed because of pollen or peanut dust. And while there's everything from."
A male voice speaks, "over-the-counter pills to EpiPens to help mitigate the symptoms. We've never been able to knock out allergies entirely."
A person speaks: "But thanks to some researchers over at Johns Hopkins, we just got crazy close to eliminating these things once and for all." This is followed by a short, low musical note.

A male voice speaks clearly, "So, allergies basically occur when your immune system thinks that something normal is a threat. It makes these antibodies called immunoglobulin E to protect you from things that cause illness. An allergic person's body makes way too much of it."

A male speaker says, "And these antibodies, they bind to mast cells, and together they absorb chemicals from your blood that are helpful in fighting invasion. And when something like pollen gets into an allergic person's bloodstream, it sticks to the antibodies and the mast cells release all those chemicals, like histamine. That's the one that gives you all the itchy, runny nose, can't breathe, swelling up sort of reactions, which is why allergy medicines are antihistamines."

A person speaks in a clear, energetic voice, "allergies can also change over time. So maybe you weren't lactose intolerant when you were younger, but now, whoops," followed by a cartoonish "boing" sound.

A man speaks in a clear, informative tone: "No more ice cream for you or maybe you could never have ice cream and now you're totally good. But why? As always, it's genes. If one of your parents is allergic to something, your chance of having some kind of allergy is about 50%. Two allergic parents, 70 to 80%. But other factors"
A male voice speaks, "factors come into play. Pollution in the environment, your diet, even your emotional health."

A person speaks, "which makes it sound like some of that epigenetic stuff we've been talking about lately, right? Like maybe every allergy is connected to some specific gene sequence and environmental trigger. Well, the team at Johns Hopkins just found out that no, one single genetic pathway is responsible for a huge number of common food and environmental allergies."
A person speaks, saying, "One stupid protein," followed by a thud.

A male voice speaks clearly, saying, "called TGF beta is causing all of our problems. Now, TGF beta controls how cells in your vital organs grow and how they communicate with each other. Faulty signaling from it has been known to cause connective tissue disorders."
A male voice speaks, "But here's what's awesome. See, right now, a lot of people are using expensive prescription medicine or injections to treat allergies."
A man speaks in a clear voice, "but high TGF beta signaling can be treated with something called losartan, which is a very old, simple drug that's been used for years to control high blood pressure."
A male voice speaks, "Now, more study has to be done of course, but how awesome is that? If your body wants to make something simple like cat hair deadly, well then you can use somethings..."
A man speaks, "simple to get it back in line. And in the future, just like anything genetic, we might be able to nip this in the bud and use some sort of gene therapy."

A male voice speaks, "or future medication to change the way TGF-beta works in our bodies entirely and say goodbye to allergies forever." A rustling sound is heard, followed by more speech, "That's pretty cool. You guys have any allergies? Let's share stories of suffering down below and remember to subscribe for more DNews."

Energetic rock music plays, featuring electric guitars, bass, and drums.
Energetic rock music is playing.

Upbeat electronic music plays, followed by a male speaker saying, "My name is Jamal. I'm a student at East Detroit. If you could tell the public one thing about climate change, what would it be?" A female speaker responds, "Wow, Jamal, great question. What everyone needs to know about climate change is that it's our children and our grandchildren, many yet unborn, who are going to pay the price for climate change. And as a mother, just as I love my children, I want to provide for them and keep them safe from harm, I am fighting climate change so that they will inherit a planet that will sustain them long after I'm gone."

Rhythmic, percussive electronic music plays. A female voice speaks, "My name is Mickey Thompson and I'm a tenth grader at H. D. Woodson. Does global warming affect humans or animals more?" The music plays again briefly, followed by another female voice speaking, "Hello Mickey, my name is Mariel Pesquera and I'm a biologist at the USGS. A woman speaks, saying, "like these, there are many other examples where you can see climate change will impact both humans and animals. I hope I answered your question."
