audio_captions: Synthesized music plays and then fades as one person asks, "Darren, how are you this morning?" A second person replies, "I'm good. How are you, Dan?" The first person says, "I'm spectacular. All right. Uh, why now and where are we going with these uh with advertising on jerseys?" The second person answers, "It would have happened sooner actually. In 2011, uh, that's when Adam Silver, who obviously wasn't commissioner at the time, kind of broached the subject and said, 'Hey, you know, it's worth 100 million dollars a year to us.' And it slowed down by five years only because with the next TV deal, which was obviously signed last year coming up for the following starting next year, uh, they the the TV partners, Turner and and ESPN had at least expressed some skepticism about what happens."

A person speaks, saying, "if someone who doesn't advertise with us uses putting an ad on a jersey or putting their logo on a jersey as a way to get around us. And if we're paying billions of dollars, that's not good. So that kind of slowed things down a little bit. And then after the deal was done, um, you know, I think that they said this is not really that big of a deal. Um, and uh, and they were able to move forward. Of course, fans still think this is very much a big deal and, you know, you can go back to when naming rights started on baseball stadiums or whatever. I mean, even as late as, you know, 2000 when the when the Tigers moved to their new stadium and it's called Comerica Park and people come out and say, 'Not only am I not going to a Tigers game, I'm withdrawing my money from Comerica Bank. I'm livid.' And that's just how it is. I mean, that's that's people have to get used to it, and I think it's gonna be the same thing here." Another voice asks, "What will the jerseys look like?" The first speaker replies, "It's gonna be a two and a half by two and a half inch patch. There is no exception to that." A question follows, "Is it similar to the Kia logo for the All-Star game?" The first speaker responds, "Yes, yes. Actually the Kia logo was a little bit bigger. Um, but yes, it's gonna be that small. Um, and uh, one sponsorship evaluation company says, you see it in a in that one particular All-star, obviously is the only time that we've been able to see it, but in that one particular game, there was four minutes and 20..."

A man with a slightly compressed-sounding voice says, "nine seconds where you clearly saw Kia throughout the entire all-star game. But it'll be the Nike jersey, uh, Nike logo, the swoosh, um, on one side and"

Two men are having a conversation. One says, "that's going to be the first time, I mean what's so crazy about this is that David Stern for so long, even though Adidas did the deal that they did with how much money they paid, David Stern kept saying, 'Nope, absolutely not. No Adidas logo on the jersey.' So, when Nike, uh, in '17-'18, when Nike becomes the partner, it's going to be the first time that even an apparel sponsor has their logo on, and then on the other side will be that will be that patch. And Silver says, you know, he's still estimating about 100 million dollars a year. I think that's conservative. The league asked the teams to submit kind of estimates as to how much they would make potentially. And, uh, I was told that when you add it all up, it's in between 120 and 180 million dollars a year." The other man replies, "Well, you're double dipping. You're getting Nike money and you're going to get a sponsorship as well. So, I..." The first man continues, "One of the compromises they did make was, and this was this this this happened late, one of the compromises they did make was that the logos will not be on—the Nike will, but the other logo that they're selling will not be on the retail version of the jerseys, at least that Nike puts out. If if a team wants to put special ones in the team store..."

Two men are speaking. One says, "or they can do so. But I think that was one of the compromises." The other replies, "Okay, but soccer started this way in the 80s." The first man continues, "Yeah. Yeah, and I heard you guys just talking about it. Yes. And and you even look at the the the WNBA jerseys which, you know, that started in 2009 as a little, you know, life lock on a on a Phoenix Mercury jersey and now they're the Phoenix Life Locks. And it's just what it is. That's how it's changed. I'm not sure it's gonna be that way. But obviously things changed when the money gets greater." The second man responds, "Okay. Speaking of which, the NFL. Can you see the NFL... I obviously they're kicking the tires on this as well. They want to see how this goes, but the NFL which sells everything, why wouldn't they go go in on this?" The first man answers, "Yeah, you would think. And now the NFL did what the NBA didn't, which was years ago they decided to put the sell the allow teams to sell the logos on the practice jerseys. That didn't really turn out to be any sort of experiment at all because the only time you see a logo on a practice jersey is when there's a newscast and that newscast is from a network that doesn't have NFL rights and all they do is show highlights of what happened at practice because they can't show games."

A person speaks, "The value of that is so infinitesimal that it doesn't even it didn't it didn't even serve as a test. But uh, but yeah, no, I I I would not be comfortable saying that, you know, any league is uh is is is safe from this. And I think people will, I think people will get comfortable with it. I think they will there will be some logos that are more uncomfortable than others. I mean, I think we're so used to seeing the Cokes and the Pepsis and even, you know, if you look at the the soccer. It's based on uh how weird it is and it's just like stadium naming rights. If if if it's a weird company name or a weird logo, we tend to feel dirtier about it, and I think it's going to be the same case here." Another person asks, "So the uh GoDaddy Red Sox or something?" The first person chuckles and replies, "Yeah, I'm I'm not sure what the uh but yeah, and then there's also going to be some coolness factor to some of them. I mean on the flip side, I mean I I I'm sure a lot of people would love to see the In-N-Out logo on the Lakers." A person chuckles.

Two men are having a conversation. The first man says, "That was probably a bad team, but the way I had to pick a team in California." The second man responds, "Uh, Kobe's final game memorabilia? Uh, pretty big numbers there." The first man continues, "Yeah, they sold $1.2 million worth of Kobe stuff in the arena at Staples Center, uh, which is a record on a single night breaking, uh, what is this? Is it either 2007 or 2008, uh, uh, what was it? Led Zeppelin in London selling a million dollars worth of stuff. I mean, it breaks the all-time record. I've never seen anything like it in terms of you go into a team store and it's all one player. It's never ever been that way. I mean even with the Yankees and Jeter and you know, you could buy Yankee stuff. You basically couldn't buy any Laker stuff. Not like anyone would want to at this point in the season. But, but it it was amazing and the prices were just outrageous. Uh, and and even though they were so outrageous, I think they still mispriced it and in some cases made it too low. There was a snakeskin texture type jersey that was selling for $824. It came in a box and I saw a guy walk in and he said, 'How many do you have left?' And they said, '20.' Now that they're sold out and they're never making them again, he just cornered the market." The second man says, "Good to talk to you, Darren. Thank you for joining us." The first man replies, "Always great to catch up, Dan." The second man says, "All right, Darren Rovell, ESPN Sports Business Reporter." A male voice speaks, "One of the most popular questions we get asked is how do you take out these indentations that are caused by heavy furniture? And let's analyze first what is happening to this carpeting and why it's indented and why it doesn't just pop right back up." This is accompanied by the sound of fabric rustling.

A person speaks, saying, "Carpet has a... this type of carpet is called a Saxony. It's got a twist to it. The fibers, as I showed in other videos, have a bundle that's twisted together, which causes what's called retention. When I push down on that it bounces back up pretty easily. When a something heavy has been put on top of the carpeting for an extended amount of time, what will happen is these fiber bundles will actually lay down, and they won't easily pop back up because they've been reset. That resiliency's been reset to a different position. So what we need to do is trick it back into being resilient. The fiber twist is still there. The twist that all these filaments are twisted into is still there. But now it's laying sideways. So how do we coax this back up? Let's take a look at what's going on back here and see if there's anything else that we need to look at before we start talking about correction." The speech is accompanied by the sound of carpet fibers being rustled and manipulated.

A man speaks, "On a modern carpet installation, we have a pad. This is a example pad. It's very inexpensive quality. So, generally speaking, you're going to have a higher quality pad in your home. But this is just for demonstration purposes. Notice here that the indentation goes through the backing of the carpeting too, the secondary backing. And on a pad that's been installed, you'll also see an indentation line in the pad because this is just simple foam that's compressed. And the foam itself has been crushed as well, and it's also has a memory that is that remembers this heavy furniture leg that's been sitting here. Now, this did not come out of this carpeting. So I don't have a pad to show you, but you'll see an indentation that resembles this. So we actually have two issues. We have a pad that's crushed, we also have the fiber bundles that crushed. And a third related one actually is that the backing of the carpeting is crushed as well." The speech is accompanied by the sound of fabric or foam being handled.

A man speaks in a clear, informative tone, "When we clean carpeting, we use hot water extraction from a truck mount. So it generally gets up to 230 degrees. That helps reset the fibers itself. It doesn't do much for the backing of the carpeting though, because we don't wet the backing of the carpeting when we clean. Our goal is to only clean the fibers. We don't want to get the backing of the carpeting saturated because then we have an issue with dry times. So generally we're going to take care not to get this backing wet. It may become slightly damp, and that's fine. And that'll also help this come out. But at no time will it ever be soaking when we clean your carpeting. If after we're done cleaning the carpeting, there still is an indentation left, you can always try the ice cube trick. What you'll do is just take a few ice cubes and position them in the indentation. I've seen, I've seen really heavy like waterbed marks come out really well because what'll happen is it cools down this surface with that the cool ice cube and will relax it when it dries. So it actually rewets it more than our cleaning would but not to the point of saturating into the pad, and causes this latex to expand and then contract. And so that's why if you use an ice cube, a lot of times this part will come back flat, which causes this part to come back up higher. And over time if you leave the furniture off of this, just naturally by vacuuming it's also going to help. If the ice cube trick does not work, we may be able to try a steaming method where we use a live vapor steam with a towel. And what we'll do is carefully go over this area, these areas with a live steam, which is also designed to help expand and contract this backing. That works about 80 or 90% of the time. You may still see a little bit of shadow left. And one of the reasons why is because there may be a a slight traffic area, especially if it's a rolling chair or a walk area that's slightly around this, which will might uh might make it look a little bit different than this carpeting here. uh that's not been walked on before. It is crushed but it's not been walked on. So, getting back to what we started with, we have an issue with crushing. We want to get rid of it. Usually if we clean it first, that helps the fibers relax and pull back up. It doesn't do a bunch uh a whole bunch for the backing of the carpeting though. This part, so that's where the ice cube trick comes in. After we're done cleaning, if it still drives you nuts, put some ice cubes in here. Don't take a whole tray and dump it on here. Because then you'll have a wet pad and possibly a wet subsurface. And you don't want that. Just enough to fit in this little crushed area. And if it's still there and it still is an issue for you, give us a call. We can try our steaming system and uh that generally works really, really well if the ice cube trick doesn't. Number here is 810-225-2184. Thanks."

audio_captions: Upbeat, rhythmic music with whooshing sounds plays, followed by a cheerful female voice speaking, "Hi everyone! Here on SciShow Kids, we've talked a lot about space, the stars, the planets, and even if there might be life elsewhere in the solar system." The music continues throughout.
A character speaks in an enthusiastic voice, "But wouldn't it be cool if we could have our own mini version of the solar system right in our rooms?" accompanied by gentle background music.

A person with an upbeat female voice says, "Squeaks and I thought it'd be cool to make a model or a small-scale version of the solar system to put on the wall. Do you want to join us? All you'll need are some scissors, construction paper, and some glue. You'll also want to ask a grown-up for some help. So, let's start our model by thinking big."
A voice speaks enthusiastically, "What's the biggest thing in the whole solar system? Can you think of it?"
A character speaks in a youthful voice, "I'll give you a hint. You can see it in the sky anytime during the day."

A whoosh sound is followed by a character speaking, "That's right, the sun. The sun is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. So the sun should be the biggest piece in our model, right?"
A person speaks, "But what about the planets? Do you know how many planets there are in the solar system?" followed by an "uhm" sound.

A female voice says, "If you said eight, you're right. There are four rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. These planets are called rocky planets because they're dense. And if humans were to land on them..." followed by the sound of a thud.
A person speaks, "we would be able to touch the ground."

A female voice speaks, "And all four of the rocky planets are the ones that are closer to the sun. Further out, there are four bigger and kind of fluffier planets. They're called the four gas giants because they're really big, and instead of being made of rocky stuff like Earth is, they're mostly made of gases. The gas giants are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. So let's put them in the right order from the one closest to the sun to the one that's farthest away. Mercury is first, then Venus, then us here on Earth, and then Mars. So those were the rocky planets. Now let's move on to the gas giants: Jupiter, then Saturn, Uranus, and last, Neptune. Now that we've named all of our planets and our star, let's look at the size of each. The sun is the biggest, but what's the biggest planet? That's right, Jupiter. Jupiter is more than 10 times bigger across than Earth is. Not as big as the sun, but still pretty big. The next biggest is Saturn, followed by Uranus, and then Neptune. Next in the lineup of sizes is our home, planet Earth, which is the biggest of the rocky planets. Next biggest is Venus, followed by Mars, and then Mercury, the smallest of the planets. Now to make our model. Let's pick out a few different colors of construction paper to make our planets. You can use any colors that you'd like."
A character speaking in a bubbly voice says, "Squeaks and I have our colors picked out already. So, we're going to."
A person speaks in a clear voice, "pencil to draw our planets. We'll make the sun the largest. Then we'll make eight more circles."

A woman speaks in a cheerful voice, "circles with each one being a little smaller than the last. Once our planets and the sun have been drawn out, we'll cut them out with our scissors. You can make your". A sound of scissors snipping is heard. This is all accompanied by light, upbeat background music.

A female voice speaks cheerfully, "planets even more unique by decorating them with paints, markers, or glitter. Next, we'll take a big piece of paper to stick our sun and planets on. Alright guys, can you help me with the right order of the planets?" This is accompanied by gentle, whimsical background music.

A person speaks in an upbeat tone, "We'll start with the sun. Now, which planets are closer to the sun? The rocky planets or the gas giants? That's right, the rocky planets are the closest to the sun." This is followed by a chime sound. The speaker continues, "And do you remember which is the very closest to the sun? That's right, Mercury." Another chime sound is heard.

A character speaks, "Now, how do you know which circle to use? Remember, Mercury is the smallest planet. So, you just pick your smallest circle." This is all accompanied by a light, upbeat musical track.

An energetic female voice speaks, "Following Mercury is Venus. And Venus is the third smallest planet. So, line your planets up and pick the third smallest. Next comes home sweet home, Earth, the biggest of the rocky planets, also the fourth smallest. And the next planet in line is the last rocky planet in our solar system, Mars, which is the second smallest circle you've made. All right, can you name the first gas giant?"

A cheerful female voice says, "If you guessed Jupiter, you're right. It's the biggest planet in our solar system. So, grab your biggest circle." A soft plopping sound is heard. The voice continues, "After Jupiter comes Saturn, and I'm going to draw some really cool rings around mine," accompanied by a scribbling sound. The speech continues, "because Saturn is famous for its beautiful rings. Next in line is Uranus, which also has really cool rings."
A high-pitched voice speaks, "the furthest planet from our sun and also the smallest gas giant, Neptune." Upbeat, synthesized music plays in the background.

A character speaks in an enthusiastic voice, "And voila! You have your very own little solar system to hang up with pride and show off to your friends. Thank you so much for helping Squeaks and me make the solar system. Did you make your own? We'd love to see it. Grab a grown-up and send an email to kids@thescishow.com or leave us a comment below. And we'll see you next week." This is followed by upbeat electronic music.

audio_captions: A man speaks, "John Gibbons, field manager of the Toronto Blue Jays. How you doing, sir?" Another man replies, "I'm doing good. I'm a little bit shocked though. I got some..."

A man speaks, "Tuesday, you know, a better a great friend Jerry, you know, and uh, but I understand he's on the air right here with us, huh?" Another man replies, "He's right here." A third man says, "John, uh, I would have reached out to you."

A man speaks, "along with some others, but somehow we're able to keep this a secret until 9 o'clock this morning, but let me just say here first of all, John Gibbons is one of my best friends and what he does in his life outside of baseball is admirable, patience, family, and that's what attracted me to John in the beginning and his outlook on the game of baseball and how he also gets players respect and they play hard for him. And John, I appreciate all that in you and now I'm the one who's starting to get emotional because of our friendship." Another man responds, "Geez Jerry, I I appreciate all those kind words and you know, we go back we go back a long way. I mean you go back further, you know, with most of the fans at Toronto, Canada, but you know, it's just been it was an honor to meet you years ago and we did we came very very good friends and you know, deep deeper than baseball ever was, you know. We went beyond that and shared a lot of things together and and, you know, you know, went through some ups and downs together and you've always been a big supporter of mine and I will never forget that and uh, you know, the beauty of your baseball career, Jerry, you always called it like it is, man. You uh, you never sugar coated anything but you were always fair. And uh, you know, I I I just hope I see you around quite a bit. We'll we'll stay in great touch but I hope I hope you still come out to the ballpark quite a bit." The first man replies, "Well, I will. I'll tell you a funny story too, Jeff, with John on the line here. When JP Ricciardi took over, he brought John in as a friend. They were together in the Met system and roommates when they first started, I believe in 1980. And so John was out in the bullpen, he was a bullpen catcher because Ricciardi eventually knew what he wanted to do with John. So then John was the first base coach. So that first year, Carlos Tosca was the manager and I kept talking to Carlos at the batting cage. And then one day Tosca left and up to my elbow comes John Gibbons and he looks at me and he says, 'Jerry, you know, I know some baseball too.'" This is followed by laughter. The man continues, "And that's... a very little but a little..." Laughter is heard again. He goes on, "That started our friendship and we both kind of laughed out loud because we really hadn't really had an opportunity to talk with one another. But then John told me too, he said, 'Jerry, remember, in baseball, you can talk about..."
A male voice speaks, "about anything. It's not black and white. There's always"

A person speaks, "something you can talk about. It's always a game you can debate, you can go over the strategies. It's never set in concrete terms. Talk to me about anything and everything because that's what baseball is. And I never forgot that because that lent itself to all kinds of conversations where other managers sometimes would be a little standoffish and say, 'We're not going there,' or, 'I can't talk about that,' or, 'I don't particularly want to hear about that story from last night.' Well, John was never that way. John is was as open with me as he is his players and coaches and that's what makes John special." Another person then says, "John, the the relationship..."

A man speaks, saying, "between the the club broadcaster and manager, um, is is a special one, isn't it? And people, you know, like I always I always tell people, it's, you know, when when you travel with the team, when you get to see guys in the charter around the hotel, when you get to talk to them, you accumulate a lot of things that quite frankly other people have no business knowing. Um, it it's an important relationship for a manager, isn't it though? The club broadcaster so that you don't want any mixed messages getting out." Another man responds, "Right. Yeah, no no doubt, and you know, we're with each other every day, and you know, that's that's where, you know, Jerry and I had something different."

A male voice speaks, "you know, we we were we were good friends, you know, we enjoyed being around each other. You know, it just wasn't all baseball, you know, it was, you know, he took a, you know, big interest in my family, you know, and and uh, he, he did, he he he he does, you know, he's not he's still still here, he's not going anywhere. But um, yeah, and and you you could always trust him, you know, because um, you know, yeah, they see things on the field that you know, that are, you know, that that goes on with the team that you know, everybody doesn't need to know about and uh, but she had to be able to trust trust trust those individuals and but there was just something we hit it off. I I can't".
A man speaks, "...we totally explain everything. You know, Jerry would always every day..." A click sound is also heard.

A man speaks, saying, "comes to the ballpark with enthusiasm, you know. Not everybody every day is gonna do that. You know what I mean? I don't come in every day enthusiastic quick. But Jerry always did and you know, that brings a smile to the guy's face and you know, we didn't, we didn't always agree on everything. We had our moments like, like everybody does. But you know what, he always picks you up and he always, I knew one thing, he was, he was always going to give it his best effort that night on the air and I know all his fans out there over the years can truly appreciate that because that's what he did. He was always prepared. Um, you know, it's just a, I'm sad, I'm sad today. You know, uh, you know, like, like everybody else out there is and uh, but we'll uh, you know, we'll see plenty of each other. We'll uh, you know, Jerry and I love going to movies, you know, I'm sure we'll go to some movies together because we both actually live pretty simple lives." A second man replies, "That's right. We, John and I like just the basic every dayness of life. Take it in, go with the flow, put your head on the pillow at night and say, thank you, that was a great day and let's move forward. John also said something right there too. You can be best friends with somebody as we are, but you're still going to have on occasion your moments because when you're up in the booth, things have to be said in certain ways and so when John says that, the thing I really appreciated about him is that when there were a couple of moments like that, you quickly get past them because you talk it over real fast and you see, well, this is where I was coming from and this is where I was coming from. But the best part of all of that is that when John would share information with me, then when I went on the air and confidently used it as my own, I knew it had a purpose. I knew it meant something, rather than Jerry just going off on his own tangent." A third speaker adds, "You've got to know what not to say as well as what to say." The second man continues, "And John always made that easy for me too, but overall, when you look at his body of work and mine, two professionals who really did the very best they could each day and that's all you can ask." The third man then says, "And John, I just got to jump in here because you're not…"

There goes our friend."

A man says, "If you just call those my nursing shoes." Another man speaks amidst laughter, "It's the only other place I've seen them. It's the only other place I've seen them too, so." The first man replies, "Yeah, no, I only wear them on, I only wear them on getaway days, all the rest would be my uh, sketchers."

Two men are laughing. One says, "happy about that and see John and I are able to laugh with each other and his laugh, I can almost imitate his laugh like some people can imitate my voice and but John, let me just say this um, I won't be in spring training. I will be there opening day because I want to see Brandy Halladay, who I've known for years. I'll see you then and many times down on the field, but John, you are one of the the best inspirations for me and friends that I've ever had in my life, let alone baseball." The other man replies, "Well Pat I really love you man and uh I'm going to miss you after daily. I'm just worried I'm just worried for Mary that she's got a."

Laughter is heard as a man speaks, "...every day. That's what we need to... we need to pray for. So... yesterday. It's been a pleasure, pal. It really is." Other speakers respond, "Yeah, Mary's already...", "Take care, John," and "Yeah, and say hi to Jolie for me." The first man replies, "You got it. Thank you." A single guitar chord is played.

audio_captions: A series of electronic beeps and whirring sounds is followed by a male voice speaking, "In this video, I will show you how to make this magnetic levitator. You will need..."
A male voice speaks, "a pencil".

A person speaks: "plastic cards, four small neodymium magnets, another four larger magnets, a piece of glass, and two blocks of wood of the size indicated in the figure. I used these blocks from a Jenga game that are useful for many projects." This is followed by the sound of a small object being placed on a surface.
A male voice speaks, "Sharpen your pencil and cut the tip," followed by the sound of a pencil being sharpened. The voice then says, "Now, glue two of the small magnets to the tip of the pencil."
A man speaks, "glue the pencil again and then make another cut."

A man with a calm, instructional voice speaks. "Another pair of magnets need to be glued to the back of the pencil. This distance has to be the same as the distance between the magnets." He then says, "Use white glue to join together the two pieces of wood," followed by, "Use super glue to join the large magnets to the base." Lastly, he explains, "This is the finished base. The magnets at the back must be at a larger distance than the magnets at the front."
A male voice speaks, "The plastic cards can be sanded like I did to eliminate the color, or you can also paint them any color you like," followed by a clinking sound.

A man with a calm, instructional voice says, "The piece of glass is glued to the plastic card with hot glue or epoxy on both sides. I have also added these plastic pads to the base. We now have all the elements of the levitator, so let's try it. Put the pencil carefully. You have to find the right distance where the piece of wood has to go. Once you find the correct placement, you have to glue the wood to the plastic base." Throughout the speech, there are subtle sounds of small objects being handled and moved.

A person speaks in a clear voice, "We have glued the wood into the plastic base, and now the levitator is functional. It is stable. You can move it carefully, and the pencil will not fall. The second plastic card can be used to cover the magnets and give a better visual effect."

A male voice speaks: "In order for this to work, you have to place the magnets all with the same polarity. For example, if you glue this magnet with north south, then the other also have to be north south, north south, and north south." The voice continues, "And the same for this: north and south, north and south," accompanied by a tapping sound. He concludes, "Otherwise, it won't work." The audio ends with a short musical sting.
A sustained, synthesized musical chord plays.

A man speaks, "She believed their reasoned approach would enable France to avoid all-out civil war and save the country from ruin."

A man speaks, "Jean-Paul Marat was particularly influential and powerful during the infamous Reign of Terror, as he could use his newspaper."

A male voice speaks, "It took two attempts, but Corday finally gained entry to Marat's home on the evening of July the 13th, 1793 by claiming to have knowledge of a Girondist uprising. This is accompanied by a low, continuous humming sound.

A male voice speaks clearly, "This was likely due to a debilitating skin disorder that he might have picked up from hiding from his enemies in Paris sewers. A male voice speaks, "As promised, Charlotte gave Marat a list of people involved with the Girondist cause." The sound of rustling paper is heard. audio_captions: Upbeat, rhythmic background music plays, then a woman speaks, "I remember a time in education when decisions were made at the top, filtered down through various levels of hierarchy to classroom teachers who were expected to do something with the bits of information they received through the pedagogical game of telephone. And it's no longer like that. Connectivity has given us new new tools and new powers and it's now possible for a globally connected classroom teacher to drive change across a system. So what do we do with this power? And how do we use these tools? And what does it mean for leadership? Dennis Mycka of the literacy and numeracy secretariat, he's just retired, says that our current models of leadership in education, it's time for them to change. They're no longer, they've taken us as far as they can take us and we need to create something different in leadership if we're truly to transform our schools into places of knowledge creation. And so I'm here today to share a project in my board, the Hamilton-Wentworth District School Board, our integrated thinking project, as to show you a model of what this new model of new form of leadership might look like. And it's very much connected to my own personal journey of transformation in education. Five years ago, I decided to become a learner alongside my students, and as we discovered the power of connectivity. And we connected globally with some remarkable people and my students were able to engage in some incredible projects that weren't just being done for the sake of school but that had impact upon the world. My students ended up winning two national awards, they garnered a great deal of media attention, and I suddenly found myself as a teacher with a voice in my board and a voice in education. One of many formerly anonymous teachers who through connectivity are suddenly able to drive change in a different way in education. And one of the people I connected with through the work that I was doing was a woman named Noga Kornberg from the Rotman School of Management in Toronto. And they have a K to 12 initiative in their business school. And many people might think, what's a business school doing messing about in elementary education? But one of the graduates, Eli Avishai of Rotman said to the Dean that the that the problem solving and thinking strategies being taught at the MBA levels are almost too late. These need to be taught to a younger group of students and so they decided to enter into elementary education and I was invited to participate. And what I saw there was remarkable because for me after taking my students through amazing projects in inquiry, this was the missing piece. These were tools and a ways of approaching problem solving that would cause my students to think differently and actually allow them to come up with new and innovative solutions to very, very complex problems. I was so excited by what I saw, I immediately went back into my classroom and began experimenting and doing what I do, I blogged about it, which got the attention of Rotman and established a lovely working relationship between my students, myself, and the School of Management as we figured out what to do with integrative thinking in the classroom. My Vice Principal Audrey Hensen and my principal Barry Morlog were so amazed by what they were seeing in my students that they decided to invite Rotman into the school and release the entire middle school staff for a day of training in integrative thinking. And then I did something I never would have done five years previously. I contacted my director because now I could. Connectivity is changing the way working relationships happen in education."

A female voice speaks, "And I felt comfortable letting him know what was happening in my classroom, that something powerful was going on. And I connected him with Ellie at Rotman, and he ended up taking the entire executive council."

A woman speaks in a clear, presentational tone, "for a day of integrative uh thinking training uh at the Rotman School of Management." Someone coughs softly. The woman continues, "So Audrey Hensen and I after all of this decided we needed to bring this in a larger way to our school board. So we put a proposal together, but we wanted to do something different, something that was meaningful, something that would be actually useful to teachers and students and be something that we could we could celebrate. So we thought about all the things that we didn't like about traditional PD and what we did. And we thought about all the things of value in these new forms of of uh PD that were happening, things like Ed Ed camp and that were happening because of connectivity and we put our model together. And the first thing we decided that this could not be the consultants receiving training in integrative thinking, uh it had to be teachers working directly with students in the classroom because they would be the ones who would see the process, see the impact of that process, get the excitement and cause this to grow. So we asked that it be teachers who get the training. And then we thought about, well, what kind of teacher would"
A person speaks, "best to take advantage of this and leverage this and grow it. And we thought those teachers already involved in transformative practice in their classrooms."

A woman speaks, saying, "should be invited to join in. So principles were asked to look for those informal leaders in their in their schools and invite them to participate. There would be nothing mandatory about this. And then we looked at the structure of how this should be, and we saw value both in formal leadership and in formal um PD and in informal PD, and how could we create something new and interesting that would leverage everything that we knew about good training. And so we knew there would be three days of a formal training with Rotman, but then we wanted to create a space in between where we could just gather as a group and share our experiences and what was happening in our classrooms and talk about what we were trying out and support each other as we grew this initiative. And then we also wanted to create an online space. So a blog was was suggested where everybody could post in one place the amazing work that we knew would happen in that classroom. We also thought that if we were going to do all this work in integrative thinking, it would be wasted unless the high schools knew the new kind of student they would be getting because integrative thinking does change how students approach learning and problem solving and wouldn't be a shame wouldn't it be a shame if that just disappeared. So we broke down the silo and asked that elementary and high school be brought together and that we move through this process together, so there's greater continuity and understanding of each other's context."

A woman speaks clearly, "And finally we thought about what kind of experience do we want teachers to have in this. And we wanted this to be a joyful, low-pressure learning experience where they would be explicitly given permission to take risks, to experiment, just try things out."

A woman speaks with a clear voice that has a slight echo, "and see what would happen with integrative thinking. That was very, very important to us and we knew from our experience with with uh Ed Camp, this was a great way for teachers to learn. So, we put our proposal into the board, it was accepted, and remarkable things began to happen. Our first group of teachers of 20 teachers have just completed uh their training and integrative thinking. And the common response or or comment I get from the teachers who've gone through it is, it's not just transforming what happens in their classroom, but it has been personally transformative. It's changing their lives, it's changing how they approach education." There is a sound of someone swallowing liquid. She continues, "It's changing how they interact with others. And uh one teacher said she's even changing her direction as a teacher because this has had such a powerful impact on her. The project has been so successful that the board has decided that a second cohort of teachers will begin training this spring because they want to grow grow this very, very rapidly. Um, on Friday, we brought together all those new teachers, the ones who've gone through the training already."

A woman speaks, "the principals who've kind of been on the outside of watching what's been happening to one space where those who've gone through the process of attempting to do integrative thinking in their classrooms to share what we've learned so far. And John Malloy, our director, spoke to us at that event. He spoke for about 15 minutes, was very inspiring. But what struck me was his message that his recognition of the importance of grassroots in education, and that we need to let these kinds of initiatives emerge and bubble up. And administration at the top needs to figure out a way to support and then get out of the way so this good work could continue to happen. And that was such a different message from ones I've received previously in education that I was really inspired and excited to hear this. So I would say to those formal..."

A woman speaks clearly, "um people in positions of formal leadership out there, that if you really want to create places of knowledge building and knowledge creation in your schools and change the culture, look to your informal leaders. See the good work that they're doing. How are you leveraging them? How are you breaking down the barriers to communication so that things can begin to bubble up and emerge. And I would say to those teachers who are doing amazing work in their classrooms to don't stay so isolated. audio_captions: A male voice speaks, "Couple discovers mysterious box buried in the woods, leaving them speechless." This is followed by ambient synthesized notes. The voice then continues, "Treasure hunting isn't just for pirates anymore. Many people love to spend their free time searching for long-lost valuables hidden deep beneath the Earth. With the use of modern metal detectors, it's never been easier to discover riches which otherwise would have been lost forever."

A male narrator speaks over dramatic background music: "When one couple was enjoying their favorite hobby, they ended up finding something that would not only leave them speechless, but change their lives forever. Ryan and Lisa loved treasure hunting in their off-time and often went on the hunt."

A man speaks, "Ryan is a pastor at the New Life Community Church in Bunker Hill, West Virginia, and loved the fact that Lisa was as thrilled as he was to search for riches." This is accompanied by gentle background music.
A male voice speaks, "When their metal detector started beeping uncontrollably, they knew they'd hit the jackpot."

A man speaks, "Lisa, especially, wasn't expecting to find such an incredible discovery on one of her first hunts. As they began digging up what the metal detector told them was buried deep beneath the earth, anticipation started flowing. Excitement filled the air as they were almost ready to uncover it. They weren't going to get their hopes up." This is all accompanied by a gentle musical score.

A man speaks in a calm, narrative tone, "as they knew there was a possibility of a false alarm. Not only could there be a false alarm, but there was also a chance that the detector was just picking up on something small, like a nail or a coin. As Ryan continued to dig, they realized they might have actually stumbled upon something worth a lot of money." This is accompanied by gentle piano music.

A male narrator speaks, "The first thing they found was an antique coin dating back all the way to the 1800s. This discovery was one of a kind and they couldn't believe they were this lucky. But this wasn't the only thing they found, however," accompanied by subtle, ambient music.

A man speaks, "They weren't sure what the coin was worth or if it was worth anything at all, but they really didn't care. In their hands, they held a piece of American history, and that alone was exciting. They decided to keep walking and to check out more locations to see if they could uncover anything else. Things were about to get very exciting." This is accompanied by soft, atmospheric music.

A man narrates, "Like a lucky charm, Lisa was holding onto the coin while she walked around with a metal detector. Flipping it around in her hand, all of a sudden they started to hear loud beeps again." This is accompanied by gentle background music and followed by loud beeping sounds.

Gentle, thoughtful music plays as a man narrates, "They'd found another treasure. Excitement filled their hearts as they began to dig again. This time they knew it was something much bigger than the first discovery. Lisa started squealing while Ryan started to uncover their newest find. He asked her to start recording because he knew this was going to be something special. The treasure was hidden beneath a medium-sized rock. Uncovering it wasn't going to be easy, but it was definitely going to be worth it. They assumed because it was hidden under a rock that whatever it was must have been valuable, and they were right."

A narrator speaks, "This could be the find of a lifetime, Ryan exclaimed, as he continued to dig. It was hard work, and Lisa knew it. 'Careful, babe,' she said. After a few minutes, they hit something hard."
A person says, "When they reached the surface of the object, they realized it was a wooden box of some kind." This is accompanied by a gentle melodic sound.

A narrator speaks: "They weren't sure how old it was, but they were hoping it would have something amazing inside. Brushing off the top of the box, they started opening it. Usually, when someone buries a box, it has mementos such as photographs, letters, and things that remind them of fond memories. Whatever was inside, they knew someone wanted to keep it, and they felt honored to be discovering it. Little did Lisa know she was in for the surprise of her lifetime." This is accompanied by gentle background music.

A narrator says, "When they took the lid off, the first thing they noticed was the box had letters in it. They weren't the type of letters they were expecting, like a handwritten note, but instead there were letters engraved on the box. As Ryan began to read them aloud, Lisa gasped with surprise." This is accompanied by subtle atmospheric music, followed by a single chime.

A gentle piano melody plays as a male narrator speaks, "Lisa thought the letters and numbers spelled out a special date and saying, and in a way she was right. When she looked a little closer, she noticed it was a Bible verse. Ryan always carries a Bible with him, so he ran to grab it out of his backpack. Both of them are religious people, so naturally, they thought this was a sign from God." The sound of pages turning is heard as he continues, "Flipping through his Bible, Ryan went in search of the matching Bible verse. The first verse was Matthew 13:44. Ryan read the verse to Lisa. The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man found it, he hid it again, and then in his joy went and sold all he had and bought that field. Lisa started to feel that this was no coincidence at all, but something more along the lines of faith. Next, Ryan read Proverbs 18:22. He who finds a wife finds what is good and receives favor from the Lord. Right after he finished reading the Proverbs, he picked up a smaller brown box that was inside. It was then that her shock grew into joy. When Ryan opened the small box, a gorgeous engagement ring was staring right back at Lisa. The letters on the box spelled out none other than Ryan and Lisa's name. It all came together. Ryan was proposing to Lisa. It was a dream come true for both of them and they were ready for their next adventure. Of course, Lisa said yes, beaming with love and excitement. She couldn't wrap her head around what had just occurred. The ring was an heirloom diamond that Ryan had received from his grandmother, a special gift that was now Lisa's. He'd put this entire adventure in motion, keeping the excitement going the whole time without her knowing a thing."
A person speaks, "What he said next was the most romantic thing she ever heard," accompanied by gentle, melodic background music.

A male voice speaks, "Ryan went on to say, 'Lisa, you're the treasure that I found in a field, and I want to give over everything that I have so I can have you.' Almost overnight, the video of their proposal went viral. Many were inspired by the creativity and the love that they obviously shared for each other." This is accompanied by gentle background music.

audio_captions: Upbeat instrumental music plays. A female voice says, "This is a fun little paper bag."

A woman speaks, "pumpkin craft you can do around the fall. All you need is one paper bag per child, couple of sheets of newspaper, our printable leaf templates from our Thanksgiving page, and an orange marker or paint and some raffia. And the first thing you want to do is show the children how to open up the brown bag and then to take their newspaper and crumple up a few sheets and stuff it down into the bottom. And you don't want it to be too packed in because you want it to add a little fluff to your pumpkin. So once that's down in there, you just want to show them how to gather together the top part. And you can play..."

A woman speaks in a calm, instructional tone: "rubber band around it to hold it if you want to. Or you can have the children..." A throat-clearing sound is heard. The woman continues, "hold it while you tie. Then if you're using markers, you can let them just start to decorate their pumpkins."
A person speaks in a clear voice, "I kind of like to use paint because it shows up a little bit better on the brown paper bags, but I know you can buy white uh lunch bags too."

A woman speaks, "So, um, also with our printable leaves, you just want to punch a hole in them and I just uh ripped off the stems just because it um it makes it a little bit easier when you're tying it around the pumpkin. And with the raffia, you just want to thread it through the holes and if you have the children do this, um just put a little piece of tape on the end and it'll kind of make it easier for them to get it through the leaf. And then you just want to have children think..." This is accompanied by the sound of paper rustling.

A female voice says, "things that they're thankful for and you can help them write on the leaves or they can write. So we're just going to write I am thankful for family. And then now that's ready to go around the pumpkin."

A person speaks, "So, after the pumpkins dry, you can, um, just take the raffia and tie it around. And I just tie, um, just a simple bow. It usually stays pretty good. Um, but if you want, you could make, um, yourself like a little loop or something if you were planning on hanging them around the classroom or something like that. So, they make good decorations. So, have fun." This speech is accompanied by rustling sounds and is followed by a short musical jingle.
A piece of instrumental music featuring a piano plays.

There's a few different ways you can hook up a soundbar to your TV, and in this video, we're going to talk specifically about using an HDMI cable. If you're looking to hook it up with an optical cable, make sure to check out our other video on how to hook up your soundbar to your TV with an optical cable. For this video, we've gone with all Samsung products, so your results may vary slightly, but remember, if you purchased your soundbar from Apt, you get lifetime technical support, so feel free to call into our service department and they can help walk you through the whole process as well. Now, hooking up with an HDMI cable is very similar to using an optical cable, it's just a different looking plug and it offers some advantages over the optical cable too. First things first though, make sure your TV and your soundbar's power cords are plugged in."
A man speaks, "Now, here's what an HDMI connection looks like," followed by a swooshing sound.
A male voice states, "The connection on your TV is going to be the same size and shape."
A person speaks, "And just like the optical cable, there's only one way that this will fit in, so there's no risk of plugging it in the wrong way. Now here's where it gets a little tricky though."

A person speaks, "When you look at the back of your TV, you want to check and see if one of your HDMI inputs is labeled as HDMI ARC, and then look at the back of your soundbar and make sure that it has an output labeled HDMI ARC."

A person with a clear male voice speaks, "In some cases, they have it, but it's not labeled. So make sure to check your instruction manual if you don't see that acronym on the units themselves. What this means is that your HDMI point ports have audio return channel capabilities, which can send sound back and forth between your TV and your soundbar. If both products have that feature, it's best to use those ports. And that's what we'll be focusing on in this video since most newer TVs and soundbars have those type of connections available. Now that you've identified the input and output on your TV and soundbar, you'll want to plug in an HDMI cable between those two. You'll also want to make sure your other components like your cable box or your Blu-ray player are plugged in, ideally also with HDMI cables and here's where having that audio return channel comes in handy. You can"
A male voice speaks, "connect your components either to your TV or to your soundbar, since the two components can send the sound back and forth to one another if needed."

A person speaks, "Once you have your components hooked up, turn on your TV and your soundbar using the buttons either on the units themselves or the power buttons on their respective remotes. Now that they're both on, you may notice another nice thing about using HDMI as your connection. It'll often times tell the TV that there's a soundbar plugged in, and it'll default to the soundbar automatically, which it does for our example here."

A man with a clear voice speaks, "If not, you're going to want to go into the sound settings on your TV and choose the external speaker option. You may need to consult your instruction manual to find out the exact term that your particular brand uses, and you also may."
A person speaks, "need to use the input button on the TV's remote to get to the input where the HDMI cable is plugged in if it doesn't happen automatically." A musical chime plays.
A person speaks, "Now that the units are talking to each other through HDMI..."
A man speaks in a clear, instructional voice, "You'll be able to control the volume using just your TV's remote if you choose."
A person speaks, "you'll also need the remote that comes with your soundbar if you want to".
A person speaks, saying, "change inputs or sound settings outside of just volume. But for basic use, your TV remote's going to work just fine." This is followed by a brief musical flourish.

A man speaks in a clear and steady voice, "And that's really all there is to it. A whooshing sound effect is followed by upbeat electronic music.

Upbeat music plays, followed by a man speaking. He says, "So we start off with the components. Here we have the smartphone with the one shield app on it. We have an Arduino Uno board with one shield on top of it, a relay board, a breadboard, this uh awesome fan, and a USB female cable to be connected to the power of the Arduino via the relay. All right? And here we're using a relay because we want to use high current, because it's not going to it's not going to work um with the low current of the Arduino because Arduino Uno, if you get a um a high on a certain pin, it gets you like 40 milliamperes. All right? This fan requires about 500 milliamperes, that's why we're using uh the power of the Arduino directly and we're using the relay to transfer the power. Okay? So, if we go to the code, we'll see here that it's really simple, just one line of code, as usual. So we first include uh one shield library, and we declare the fan to be on pin number 11, that's where the pin is connected to the relay. And in the setup, we initialize the one shield library and we set uh the pin number 11 into output. All right? In the loop here, we get the data of the proximity sensor. So, if the value is above zero, you turn on the fan. And here the switch is active low. All right? And uh if not, just turn it off, which in this case is high. Okay? So, if we look at the app. So, here we selected the proximity sensor and as you see here, the distance is about 5 centimeters. Now the proximity sensors is just similar to the light sensor, but the light sensor gives you uh a variety of data, but the proximity sensor is only one or zero. So if I cover it, it gives me zero," while a fan whirs. "And if I remove it, that's five. All right? On." The fan whirs again, followed by a click. "and off. That's it."
Rhythmic electronic music plays.

audio_captions: A man speaks, "Hey guys, Jeff here with Martin Survival. Now many of you know that the desert is a land of extremes. We have dust storms, high temperatures in the daytime, then very low temperatures in the evening that can set you in a state of hypothermia very quick. There's also one other thing, and that's a lack of moisture. Here in the Mojave Desert, it's extremely dry and it could be very difficult to track and locate water. So today I'll take you back into this canyon and we'll try to track and find some water and who knows, maybe we'll get lucky. So stay with me and let's start our search." This is followed by an electric guitar playing a rock music riff.
A melodic electric guitar riff plays.
Upbeat instrumental music plays, featuring a bass guitar and drums.
Instrumental music plays, featuring an electric guitar, bass, and drums.
A piece of music plays, featuring an electric guitar melody accompanied by a bass guitar and drums.

A brief synthesized musical introduction plays. A man speaks, "So, there's actually a few different ways to track and locate water here in my area of the high desert. Number one is following washes and that's what I'm going to do here in just a second. The second way is looking on top of the granite boulders where there's natural indentations. A lot of the time when we have our lightning storms, it'll touch right down to the rock and it'll almost form a cup. Just a natural cup right in the middle of a granite boulder. So, you can look in those right after a rainstorm and you could find water that way. Another way here in the Joshua Tree area and even down lower into the Morongo Basin is the vegetation. Whenever you find cottonwoods or willow, mule fat, you know there's water nearby. And a lot of the time that's all earthquake, the earthquake faults pressure pushing that water to the surface." This is accompanied by the sound of wind. The sound of someone walking on gravel or dirt begins as the person continues speaking, "I'm actually heading back into this wash here. And I'm gonna see if I can't find any moisture on the ground, any water pockets or, hey, maybe even a pool of water. That'd be pretty nice. That'd be actually really nice. We'll see what we have."

A man speaks, "Okay, so I don't have a pool of water or anything like that. No pockets of water. But what I did find is a lot of moist soil. So what am I going to do? I'm going to use a stone here and kind of dig underneath the earth and see if I can't find any water." This is accompanied by the sound of digging in soil.
A rhythmic scraping sound.
A rhythmic scraping sound repeats.

A character speaks, "Okay, so definitely no water in here. Usually what I like to do is dig about 12 to 13 inches underneath the earth and see if water starts forming in the pocket. But in this case, we're just hitting a bunch of moist sand and that's no good. Would I build a solar still here? Absolutely not. I do not believe in building solar stills in any survival situation whatsoever. It's very life-threatening. Not only you burn through calories, you also blow through hydration and that is a huge, huge issue, especially here in the desert. So, solar still, no go, no water forming underneath the hole. So we'll just move on." This is accompanied by the sound of sand being moved. Upbeat electronic music begins to play.
A man speaks, "Well, this is definitely a cool find. Right behind me on this boulder here, you can see their," accompanied by rhythmic music.
A person speaks, "petroglyphs from a Native American." This is accompanied by a gentle, rhythmic background sound.

A person speaks, "one of the tribesmen that lived off of this land. So, just an awesome find and kind of gives you a little bit of assurance that you're not alone out here and their spirits are definitely with us and just a really cool thing to see out here." This is all accompanied by rhythmic music featuring percussion and a wind instrument.

The sound of rustling fabric is heard. A man speaks, "Okay, so I followed the wash a few hundred feet and went around a few bends. And as you can see, we have water. This is right in the center of this rock and like I said earlier, there's natural holes in this rock and a lot of the rain water gathered in this rock. So this is an excellent find and I'm going to take advantage of this. I'm going to fill up my canteen here in just a second. Now, of course, I want to boil this down. Now, if I don't have the means of boiling it or natural filtration or even treating it with a chemical, I'm still going to drink this. A lot of the books and manuals tell you to skip out on the water and don't drink it because of all the minerals from the rock. And that's absolutely true. But in a survival situation, short term at least, you're most likely going to find help and rescue within 24 to 72 hours. So absolutely drink this. This is definitely a lifesaver." This is followed by the sound of a metal cap being removed and then the sound of water being scooped or poured.

A person speaks, "You know, the more that I look at this hole in the rock, this is definitely made by man dating back hundreds of years ago. I'm assuming they use this hole to grind acorns and manzanita berries in here, so an Indian tribesman definitely lived off of this land. Now, how can I tell that this is made by man? Right in front of me, literally about three feet ahead, there's a boulder and that boulder has."
A man speaks, "petroglyphs all over the rock as you can see. So this is definitely a..."

A man speaks, saying, "An amazing amazing thing to find. And I got to say for the lost person in the wilderness and someone who's in a survival situation, this is definitely a gift from an Indian tribesman to find water in a hole they made hundreds and hundreds of years ago. An amazing find. This stuff fascinates me. I've seen more than one of these in different areas of the park but every time I come upon one of these, I just think back in time and what they were doing and how they lived. Fascinating, to say the least. So finding water in the desert is definitely a challenge. It is by far the toughest thing to do. We were successful today but some of these lost hikers, they aren't, and they end up dehydrating and dying from lack of water. I kind of compare finding water in the desert like primitive fire in the eastern woodlands. It's very hard and it's hit or miss. You could succeed, you could fail at it. But getting out in the environment, knowing the signs, recognizing the vegetation is very crucial to locating water, especially here in the Joshua Tree area, even in the lower Morongo Basin. It's so rare. Well, I appreciate you guys joining me for this video. I'm Jeff with Martin Survival. We'll see you in the next one."

A man kneels in a dry, desert-like landscape, holding a bundle of tinder or kindling. Small pieces of wood lie on the ground next to a log. Sparse bushes and Joshua trees are visible in the background, under a clear sky. "Wilderness Survival" is displayed on the screen.

A man in a desert-like environment demonstrates wilderness survival skills, including preparing kindling for fire starting and using a compass for navigation. He also reviews outdoor gear, specifically a large knife.
A person demonstrates and tests a knife in an outdoor environment, including close-ups of the blade, striking it against an object, and using it to split wood.
A man in a hat and sunglasses sitting and talking outdoors in a rocky, arid landscape, then walking through the same environment.
A man in a hat kneels on sandy ground surrounded by large rocks, scooping and sifting sand with his hands.
A person kneeling next to a large rock digs in sandy soil with their hands and a small shovel.
A man in a hat and outdoor attire kneels, digging into sand or dirt with his hand against a rocky background.
A man in a hat and light-colored clothing kneels and digs in sand near large rock formations, then stands in a wide, rocky canyon. A bird perches on a spiky cactus.
A man in a hat and sunglasses stands outdoors among large rock formations, gesturing towards the rocks.
A large, grey rock formation with a prominent crack and patterned surface.
A man in a hat and sunglasses stands among large rock formations and dry bushes, then carefully descends a rocky path between boulders, holding a thermos.
A man navigates a rocky, desert-like landscape, then crouches beside a large rock containing a small pool of water, demonstrating water collection from the natural basin.
A man in a hat and sunglasses leans over a large rock with a depression, gesturing and speaking, in a desert landscape with sand, sparse bushes, and large boulders under a clear sky.
Close-up view of rough-textured rock formations, slowly panning across their surfaces and crevices.
A man in a hat and sunglasses speaks to the camera, first leaning on a large rock with a depression, then seated in a rock shelter. He is in a rocky, desert-like landscape.
A desert landscape silhouette against a vibrant sunset sky, with the text "Find me on Facebook www.facebook.com/martinsurvival" overlaid.

A natural body of water with green plants growing in the foreground and abundant green trees lining the distant bank. Text overlays with production credits and contact information appear over the water scene.

audio_captions: A man says, "I mean I have a lot of faith in my young guys. Uh, I know that's why they're here. That's the reason they're here. Uh, I say sometimes fun, sometimes fun, but uh, we'll get it done." A musical transition plays. Another man speaks, "It was supposed to be the golden era of Canada basketball with golden opportunities lying ahead at the World Cup later this month. Instead, Team Canada will look for diamonds in the rough again and hope this roster is good enough to earn them an Olympic birth for the first time since 2000. Let's bring in Michael Grange, who you can read on sportsnet.ca. Michael, this has been a very divisive, obviously, conversation. It's hard to fault players when they say, 'Hey, they want to focus on the season.' It's hard to fault players, of course, pulling out when they have injuries right now, but you can't help but still feel disappointed given the expectations that were there to start the summer and where we kind of are now with the roster, can you?" A third man replies, "I think it's fair fair to be disappointed."

A man speaks, "this has been a moment in Canadian basketball that a lot of people have been pointing towards and a lot of the players have been pointing towards, both among the group that are in camp and the ones that aren't in camp, among the management, and you know, this is sort of this".
A man speaks in a clear voice, "the start of what should be at least a five-year cycle where Canada can emerge as a world basketball power. And this is an opportunity."

A male speaker says, "for the guys in this cohort to really make a name for themselves outside of the NBA, to really kind of uh weave their way into the the Canadian sports fabric. uh but you got to play. And uh, you know," all accompanied by a rhythmic musical beat.

A man speaks, "So it's it's it's frustrating when, uh, you know, I think it's frustrating for a lot of people when so many guys who could be difference-makers on this team aren't available to play for a number of reasons. Most of all, I think it's frustrating for the guys who have made the effort to play and are going into China a little bit shorthanded." A second man says, "There are a lot of people pointing to the schedule. This tournament starts at the end of August, finishes in the middle of September, training camp opens just a couple of weeks after. You don't buy that as a reason. So what do you think the main reason is that players are dropping out? It's not just Canadians, of course. And secondly, again, how how much is this impacting a tournament like this in the NBA in general when all these top-tier players don't want to participate for country?" The first man replies, "Well, I think the the the swath of it, the main country that's been affected is the US of course."
A person hums a short note, "Hmm." Another person speaks, "... is in the lead."

A man speaks, saying, "different category. They they could probably send players, you know, they have roughly about 300 NBA players and I think they could probably go down to their bottom 100, pick pick 10 and do pretty damn well. Um, they're nowhere near that. They still have a really good team. They're the favorites. They haven't lost a game internationally since 2006. They are going to qualify for the Olympics."

A person speaks, "So you know, the fact that some of their top stars are choosing to approach it differently, they have the option to do that because of the success they've had. A country like Canada does not have that option. Um, you know, it's a it is a deep group of NBA players. It's going to get deeper as this really young kind of tier matures. But they they don't have a pedigree. They there's no guarantee they're going to get to the Olympics. They haven't been to the Olympics since 2019 or sorry, 2000. Um, and so what it's going to take to to, like I say, make Canada, um, allow Canada to reach the potential they have internationally is guys to make make a sacrifice to really inconvenience themselves. And I I think, you know, I struggle when when people start laying out a bunch of reasons why they're not..." The speech is accompanied by the distant rumbling of traffic.

A man speaks in a conversational tone, saying, "playing, I'm not saying they're not legitimate or they're not pertinent to the individuals involved, but you know, they all all those exact same issues face the guys who are playing. And so really what you can only conclude is the guys that have chosen..."

A man speaks, "...to to pass on this World Cup in China. Uh, haven't put it high enough in their priority list compared to whatever their other priorities are. Doesn't mean them make them bad patriots, don't mean we have to take away their passports. Um, it's a very good chance that that some of those guys who aren't playing." This is all accompanied by background music.

A man speaks, "will be essential figures in a team that may have to go to a last chance qualifier next next summer to get into the Olympics. So you can't really kick him out the door, but it's just uh it's just tough that uh this this they're not going to be around this time." A second man speaks, "Well, Canada still has to compete with the roster it has, and it's one that boasts a lot of international experience, a lot of FIBA experience, which should bode well in a tournament like this. But again, what are the realistic expectations for a team like Canada without the NBA players and a tough group featuring Australia, Lithuania, and Senegal?" The first man speaks again, "Well, I think they have a good chance."

Electronic music with a steady beat plays in the background. A man speaks, "to advance out of that that first pool and they have a good chance to uh advance in the tournament. You know, I think it might be the best team Canada's ever had. I mean you have guys like Cory Joseph, Kelly Olynyk, Khem Birch, all in their prime supported by uh Chris Boucher, um who's, you know, as we know an up and coming NBA talent. And then when you comb the international pros, guys like Phil Scrubb, uh Melvin Ejim, um Thomas Scrubb, Kevin Pangos, like these are guys who are playing in the best leagues in in Europe and and maybe the best group of international pros Canada has ever had. So I think they're going to be a capable, they're going to be a good shooting team, depth at point guard, depth up front. What they're missing unfortunately is uh some scoring punch and that's where you're the likes of Jamal Murray and uh maybe RJ Barrett and and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander are really going to be felt."
A person says, "It'll be interesting to see what this Canadian team does. It'll be an interesting tournament as a whole that begins at the end of the month."
A man speaks, "Michael Grange, thanks a lot Michael. You can read him of course on sportsnet.ca."

audio_captions: A crashing sound is heard, followed by a man speaking, "Yeah, well, Des Nations is a great weekend. I mean, uh, I started off Saturday. Not too, I didn't feel too comfortable, you know. It got really rutted and stuff, but I pulled off the qualifying race and that was good. And I think all of my eyes, all of the German riders, they did pretty good, my teammates. Um, you know, we had a we had a good gate pick. It was totally enough. Then I went into Sunday feeling confident and stuff. So I had a good first moto, but I struggled the whole weekend with arm pump and I wasn't really that that happy, but um, so after that first moto, you know, I finished second. It was okay. I could have, you know, I really wanted to win that one. But um, in the second one, I actually had all good starts, so that was great. Um, coming into the last moto, I could finally ride how I wanted to ride. Had a great battle with Tomac and um pulled off the win, and I think after RV, I'm the first guy altogether with him that that um won a full moto. So that's that means a lot, and um, you know, made history. I won MX2 class four times in a row, which meant a lot to me." This is accompanied by a background murmur.
A musical chime sounds, followed by a female voice saying, "Here is your ticket."

A man speaks, saying, "No, it usually is always like that. The track just gets super rutted and the ruts are not like nice and round, they're like really weird and a lot of rocks. Um, they actually changed the track quite a bit too, but uh I had been there the year before. I just every year I just went there once because of the GP. And um a lot of it was similar but they put some sand in and um obviously there were a lot of rocks." This is accompanied by background chatter.
A man speaks in a serious tone, "They don't know who," accompanied by tense background music.

A person says, "Um, it's about an hour, an hour from my house. I don't really know if it's open all the time, but I mean, I got my track behind the house and uh we have a couple of local tracks close to my place, so that's where I'll usually be." This is accompanied by the sound of a low, rumbling engine.
A man with a deep, calm voice says, "The next time you make love with the woman you love..." This is accompanied by soft, melodic background music.

A male voice speaks, "Um, I stayed back in Europe for about three weeks. And the Red Bull Give Me Five was a super fun event. I mean, Madrid in general is a super cool city. We had a lot of fun together, everybody. The event was pretty cool. It was a different type of racing. The track was fun. And the fans were unbelievable. I mean, it got sketchy sometimes, they almost took down the whole tent. So, um, it was it was cool to see that. And after that, I flew straight to Florida." This is accompanied by background chatter.
A male voice speaks, "So, if it does not have the capacity..."

A man speaks: "Well yeah, I'm working with Aldon now and it's going to be a nice little group with Adam, Ryan and me. Um, we're going to be riding on RV's property. So, uh, I'm excited about it. Um, get all my fitness tests and stuff and just get set up and sort a few things out." A low hum is audible in the background.

A male voice says, "It definitely I have to change my diet and stuff. I mean, Chipotle is not even a thing. There's just a few things you can't take, but Chipotle in general is um all organic, like it it it's good to eat. But you just have to watch with your dairy and um in general it's going to be a very hard part for me because you know I have never been too serious about that diet thing. But um no, I do all that for the end win, you know, for the final win. So I'm I'm ready for it. I'm motivated and uh can't wait to get going." The speech is set against a backdrop of faint, ambient chatter.
A dramatic musical chord plays, followed by a man speaking in a deep voice, "How good of you to come."

A man speaks amid background chatter: "Well, obviously I'm full-time 450 now and uh I only have ridden four times now on the test track, but actually feeling pretty solid out there. Had a good first practice and overall it's my first time uh riding Monster Cup. So, it looks like it's a cool event. I'm really excited about it and I can't wait." A shattering crash is heard, followed by a thump.
