audio_captions: A fast-paced, funky electronic bassline plays.
Upbeat music plays as a man says, "What's up guys? Jeff here from Worldwide Cyclery, and today we're going to go over how wide should your mountain bike handlebars be?"
A synthesized melodic jingle plays.
A piece of light, melodic electronic music is playing.
Upbeat electronic instrumental music is playing.
A segment of electronic music plays.

Upbeat electronic music plays, followed by a person speaking, "All right, so mountain bike handlebar width. This widely depends on, well, a few factors. Uh most importantly is the riding discipline. So downhill riders are always going to want a wider bar because it's just more stable and you have more leverage. If you look at professional motocross, you're going to realize all of those guys are running a seriously nice wide..."

A man speaks, "bar. And the to talk a little bit about the evolution of mountain bike handlebars. In the early days, mountain bike handlebars were pretty narrow. Uh, road bikes were around first and aerodynamics was a pretty important thing in the road world. Um, so that's a whole different segment, right? But mountain bikes sort of evolved from road bikes, you know, decades ago. And the early days of mountain bikes, the bars were super narrow. You'll see a lot of old photos of, you know, legends like John Tomac racing and uh he's doing downhill races and World Cups and he's got these tiny little skinny bars and it looks hilarious. Um, along with a whole bunch of the other stuff on their bike. But as mountain biking evolved, people started realizing that wider and wider bars were just a lot more stable and a lot more comfortable. And I also realized that there were different disciplines. As mountain biking evolved, it got into, you know, cross-country and uh and trail riding and comfort bikes and uh and downhill bikes and freeride bikes and there's all these different types of bikes now. So different width bars will kind of apply to those. But um, you know, typically you're going to see cross-country bikes are going to have narrower bars. And a lot of that has to do with the, you know, aerodynamics is a factor. If you're concerned about that, obviously a narrower bar is going to work better because if you're like this on a bike as opposed to like this."

A man speaks in an explanatory tone, "...your chest is going to be more out and that's just an aerodynamic thing especially if your bike is more leaned forward, you probably like a cross-country bike, you're going to be more comfortable like this than you might like this. Um whereas on a downhill bike, you're a little bit more upright and again you're at really high speeds and you want a lot of control and stability. so you're going to want a you know, wider stance bar. So, if you look at, you know, World Cup cross country racing today and World Cup downhill racing, you're going to very uh easily notice the difference in the bar widths. cross-country bike."

A man speaks in a clear, conversational voice: "that are going to have much skinnier than downhill. Um, there is a a bit of personal preference in there too. So, maybe if you came from riding uh road bikes and cross-country bikes and now you ride an enduro bike or a downhill bike, you might just feel more comfortable on a narrower bar that you're used to. And typically what feels more comfortable to you is just going to be better for you. Cuz if you feel comfortable on the bike, you're going to ride good and have fun and and that's what it's about. Um if you came from motocross, like myself, I came, I rode motocross before I got into mountain biking as a kid. So I was used to a a pretty darn wide bar on my dirt bike as a kid. So when I got on my first mountain bike, I felt like they were pretty narrow. Um and I I just like felt naturally like I wanted a wider bar. So again, what feels comfortable for you is does matter. So you'll see some weird preferences. There's some different downhill pros out there that um"

A person speaks, "run pretty darn narrow bars, I guess you could say compared to the rest of their competitors. And then there's some guys who run pretty wide bars compared to the rest of their competitors. So it definitely depends on the discipline that you're doing and the type of bike that you're riding and what you're trying to do with it. And wide bars are going to be more stable and more controlled, so if you're going really fast like you are on a downhill bike typically, having a good wide bar is going to be stable and awesome."

A person speaks in a conversational tone: "And bike manufacturers have caught onto this as well. You know, I remember back in 2005, 2006, a lot of the the bikes back then were coming specked with pretty darn narrow bars and pretty long stems. And again, that's because mountain biking sort of evolved off of road biking. So a lot of the bikes, you know, the first mountain bikes out there were much more like cross-country bikes. And then as they evolved into these trail bikes, Enduro bikes, downhill bikes, they started kind of transforming more into like a dirt bike, a motocross bike. So shorter stem, wider bars, a little more upright position, slacker head tube angles. Like as as the bikes evolved, the handlebars did too."

A man speaks, "And and that's when people started realizing, you know, wow, I I feel much more comfortable. So when I was uh a mechanic at a shop as a teenager, a lot of the bikes we would sell would have like a a 680 mil or 700 mil wide bar, which in today's world is really narrow. Like you're probably not going to find any trail bike or even a cross-country bike with a bar that narrow. Um, and a long stem. And you know, the customer would come in would feel uncomfortable on it and we would slap something bigger on there, which bigger back then was like a 720, 740, um, which is still again kind of small even to today's standards. Um, but they would immediately feel, wow, I'm much more comfortable. I have a wider bar, I feel more stable, you know, I'm I'm more upright, so they felt more comfortable on the downhill. Um maybe a little less on the uphill with the shorter stem, but that's a whole different video. But the the wider bars giving you more stability is is pretty darn important and people seem to love that. Um, myself personally these days, I ride a 760. So 760 millimeters, that's 29.9 inches. Um, I like that width. I got used to that. Um, I guess you, you know, some again, it's kind of an opinion that your next C rider watching this, you're going to think that's a really wide bar. If you're, you know, a modern day downhill rider, you're going to think that might be narrow. You know, a lot of downhill riders are riding 800s or 820s even, which is like what some Race Face and DD bars come in these super wide widths. Um, I like a 760 because um, I like it consistent across all my bikes. So I have a dirt jump bike and a trail bike and a downhill bike and I ride in different areas. Sometimes I'm riding in uh Southern California and there's no trees around. Other times I'm riding out on the East Coast in Pennsylvania and there's trees everywhere."
The sound of rustling and crinkling paper.

A man with a clear, conversational voice speaks, "Um and when there's trees everywhere, I kind of like having a 760 because it's not super wide, whereas I probably would like the feel of like a 780 or an 800 better, but I just feel like it's too wide and then I'd be slamming my hands into the trees and stuff. So, I like a 760 to keep it consistent and the same across all the different bikes that I have and I ride. So that's kind of just been my personal preference and and what I stick with." A light tapping sound occurs, and he continues, "These bars right here, Race Face Next, they come 760 out of the box. So I just keep them at that length and don't need to cut them. It's kind of nice. Renthal Fatbar lights, same thing, 760 out of the box. And again, some people might consider that narrow, some people might consider that wide. Again, kind of a personal preference and in where you came from and what bike you're putting these bars on. Some of the newer bars these days, Race Face Six, these are 820 mm wide. So that's a a pretty darn wide bar. And, you know, the six line is really made for downhill bikes. So that's why they're making them super wide and you can cut them, you know, down I think all the way down to 770, as it do not cut beyond 770. So that's still a pretty darn wide bar, but it depends on what you're looking for. Another thing to factor in with bars is your shoulders. So, there's your big difference in shoulder width from a, you know, a five-foot-two rider versus a six-foot-four rider and people are just built differently. And if you have more narrow shoulders, you might feel a little more comfortable on a bar that doesn't make you feel too wide, right? And vice versa, if you've got really broad shoulders, you might like a really wide bar because it just feels more natural. Like when you put your arms out naturally, where do they fall? And that's going to be different for different shape and size people depending on your shoulders mostly and your arm length, and just personal preference there too. So, yeah, as far as bars go, a common bar, like actual just the width of it on a just let's say a general trail mountain bike these days, 760 is pretty darn common. So 29.9 in in width, that's a pretty common size bar. Once you start going smaller than that, you're kind of getting towards the cross-country range and if you go bigger than that, you're kind of towards the downhill bike range. So if you don't really know where to start, see what feels comfortable and and the cool thing is a lot of these bars, especially aluminum bars, you can cut them down a lot. So you can always just test it out, you know, see what feels comfortable for you. If you're riding something less than 760 right now, and you're not concerned about being aerodynamic and you want a little more stability, try 760 or try 780. It's I think you'll be pretty impressed. I have personally seen a lot of people, you know, get into the sport of mountain biking and ride narrow bars like 740s or under or 720s or 700s, and slap on a 760 or 780 and just fall in love with that width bar. Like I said, back in the day bikes weren't really specked with what I would say is like good bar and stem combos. They were really like long and stretched out and like cross-country focused. And that's good if you're trying to race cross-country. It's bad if you're sort of a general trail rider and you want more stability on a downhill, then a little bit shorter stem and a little bit wider bar is going to feel a lot more comfortable for you. So, yeah, that's kind of it on the bars. Let us know if you guys have any questions, what handlebars you're running, and more importantly, what width are you running and why? Uh please hit subscribe. We'd love to show you guys some more cool mountain bike content, and check out the other videos on our channel. Take it easy."

audio_captions: Upbeat electronic music with a strong dance beat plays, ending with a final musical hit.
A man speaks, "The 12th of May 2013," accompanied by the sound of a murmuring crowd.
A person speaks, "long in the memory in the French camp."
Amid the sound of a cheering crowd, a man speaks energetically, "after 19 years of hurt, Paris Saint-Germain wrapped up the title."

The sound of a crowd cheering loudly. A man says, "...league and title in their history with a 1-0 win over rivals Lyon at Stade de Gerland. A title which Paris, with their bevy of international stars, looked destined to win from the off. And yet the capital club had trouble getting out of the starting blocks." The cheering and background music continue throughout.

A man speaks, "picking up only three points in their first three games. It wasn't until the fourth game of the campaign that Carlo Ancelotti's men claimed their first win of the season and it was an important one at that. Zlatan Ibrahimovic's second brace of the season with the first goal after just 27 seconds saw Paris." This is accompanied by the sound of a cheering crowd.

A man speaks, "...on their way to a two-one win over Lille at the Grand Stade," followed by the sound of a crowd booing. He then says, "Three more wins followed in a flawless month of September. And there was another brace for the super Swede as Paris hammered Ligue 1 new boys Bastia 4-0 on the road in Corsica," accompanied by loud cheering from a crowd.
A man speaks, "Nine games in, Paris went top of the table for the".
A male voice says, "...time with a narrow win over promoted side Ross."

A male voice says, "were still a few question marks surrounding their style of play." A crowd cheers loudly. The voice continues, "And especially when they found themselves caught up in their traditional November crisis. Home defeats to Rennes and Saint-Étienne, who also knocked Paris out of the League Cup."

A man speaks, saying, "and their loss to Nice on December the 1st. So Paris dropped to fourth, five points off leaders Lyon. With Ancelotti under threat, the players held an emergency meeting in a Parisian pizzeria. And cowabunga! A vital Champions League win over Porto revitalized the club who won four league games in a row, scoring 12 and conceding none." This is all set against the sound of a crowd, which intensifies with loud cheering.

A male speaker says, "vital win over then it is Lyon, which saw them retake top spot. And with their far superior goal difference, they finished autumn..." This is accompanied by the sound of a crowd.

A narrator speaks, "ahead of Lyon and Marseille. They kept up the tempo after the winter break with four more wins on the bounce, including a 4-0 thrashing of Toulouse away from home, one of Paris's most accomplished performances of the season." This is accompanied by the sound of a crowd roaring.

A male voice speaks, "Well, the classic against Marseille wasn't quite as pretty, but Paris rode their luck with a 2-0 win over their historic rivals. A certain David Beckham making his first league one debut." This is accompanied by the sound of a crowd cheering.
A male voice says, "...parents," amidst the sound of a cheering crowd.
A male voice says, "Sometimes between...", accompanied by the sound of a crowd.
A male voice says, "in their Champions League quarter-final legs against Barcelona, Paris claimed another 2-0 win."
A man speaks, saying, "a white strugglers ran, and Jeremy."

A person speaks, "popped up with the goal that had a certain Lionel Messi-ish quality to it." This is followed by the sound of a crowd cheering. The speaker continues, "wasn't to score many this term, only five overall, but they were all important."
A male voice speaks, "And none more so of them..." This is accompanied by the sound of a cheering crowd.
A male voice says, "well-taken goal which was to seal the title for Paris against Lyon," accompanied by the sound of a cheering crowd.
A male voice speaks, "in week 36," accompanied by the sound of a crowd.
A man speaks over the sound of a cheering crowd, saying, "Seven points ahead of Marseille with two games to go."
A male voice speaks, "14 ahead of Lyon. Paris had a chance to celebrate their title at..." This is accompanied by the sound of a crowd.

A person speaks, "...against relegated Brest. Ibrahimovic fired in a seventh brace on his way to 30 goals overall, and Blaise Matuidi capped a fine season with his fifth of the campaign." This is all accompanied by the sound of a crowd cheering.
A large crowd cheers as a commentator speaks, "Paris with the best attack and best defense were simply the best, and simply the Ligue 1 champions."

Amidst the sound of a cheering crowd, a man speaks, saying, "Thiago, je te laisse faire la fête et la communion avec le public du Parc des Princes." Music then begins to play as the crowd continues to cheer and sings along.
A male voice sings the lyrics, "...my friends, and we'll keep on fighting 'til the end." This is accompanied by rock music and the sound of a cheering crowd.

audio_captions: Energetic, rhythmic electronic music plays.
Upbeat instrumental music plays, followed by a male speaker stating, "In June of 2016, the U..."
A male voice speaks, "Department of Housing and Urban Development inaugurated the first National Healthy Homes Month. The theme that year was everyone deserves a safe and healthy home."
A male voice speaks, "Today, the annual month-long celebration continues to offer an opportunity for the public to learn more about housing and its impact on health. It is also a time for".

A man speaks, saying, "agencies, such as HUD, to raise awareness and provide resources for what makes a healthy home, and to strengthen coordination and collaboration between housing and health at the federal, state, and local levels."

A person speaks in a clear voice, "This continues to be important because Americans spend about two-thirds of their time in a residence, whether it be their own home, a family member's, or a friend's, according to HUD. The agency also states that a healthy and safe home is one that incorporates the principles of a healthy home."

A man with a clear voice speaks, "These would include the following: Keep your home dry. Mold and moisture increase allergens and asthma triggers and can cause deterioration of a home. Keep your home clean. Clean homes help reduce pest infestations and exposure to contaminants. Keep your home pest-free. Many pest treatments pose risks for families with health problems or expose young children and pets to poisonous residue. Non-pesticide treatments are best for the first line of defense. Keep your home safe. A majority of injuries among children occur in the home. Falls are the most frequent cause of residential injuries to children, followed by injuries from objects in the home, burns, and poisonings. Keep your home contaminant-free. Chemical exposures include lead, radon, pesticides, and environmental tobacco smoke. Exposure to radon gas, carbon monoxide, and secondhand tobacco smoke are far higher indoors than outside. Keep your home ventilated. Studies show that increasing the fresh air supply in the home improves respiratory health. Air filters and HVAC units collect and protect families from many particulates found in the air. Keep your home maintained. Poorly maintained homes increase the risk for deteriorated lead-based paint in older housing which is the primary cause of lead poisoning in children less than six years of age. Keep your home temperature controlled. Houses that do not maintain adequate temperatures may place the safety of residents at increased risk from exposure to extreme cold or heat. These are just a few things to know about some of the indoor environmental quality issues associated with National Healthy Homes Month."
A person speaks in a clear, calm voice, "To learn more about this or other air quality, environmental, health, or safety issues, please visit the website shown on the..."

A thud sound is heard. "And one is my desktop computer. You know, you don't want to really just unplug that from the wall because they will go off and it's just not good for them. Another click sounds. "So let me hit that, just turned it off here again. So pretty heavy, this is probably going to want to be on the floor. Obviously, you're going to kind of want it to hide it away in most cases. For me, it's just on the floor by my desk where I've got my, you know, computer plugged in. There's a 5-foot power cable. You have a couple of, you know, ethernet jacks here, network out, network in, if you want that network to pass through here. You also have a power shoot USB port. I think these are for like, you know, uh printers, cameras, those type of things." Rustling and handling sounds are heard. The person continues, "And I think that's just about it. Yeah, that's pretty much all the other ports. The really the ones that you probably care the most about are these outlets on the top, which are going to be kind of universal. So, what I want to do here and just kind of show you how it works and that it does work, is I'm going to plug it in." A sound of something being plugged in is heard. The person then says, "And I have a my special light with me."

A person speaks, "What this little light does, I think I did a review on this. It's the Eton Blackout Buddy. It's just an emergency light. Um, it has a little sensor on it, uh, for one's a night light, but then the other's an emergency flashlight. If it senses, you plug it into an outlet to keep the battery charged, and when the power goes off, it it sees that the power has gone off and turns on the emergency light. When it detects power again, the light goes off. So it's going to be kind of a good little visual indicator."

A man speaks, "Now, there's something to know here is that the four outlets on this side are surge protected and the four outlets on this side are battery backup and surge protected. So it's going to silk screen down on there."
A slight rustling sound is heard, followed by a male voice saying, "So, I'm going to plug it into the..."

audio_captions: A gentle, rhythmic musical track plays as a female speaker with a clear voice says, "The world has made tremendous progress in reducing extreme poverty. But this progress has slowed down and is uneven. If this trend continues, the world will not be able to end extreme poverty by 2030. However, the extreme poverty picture shows an emerging divergence. While extreme poverty is still stubborn in some low-income countries, several others have made rapid strides in moving people out of extreme poverty. But that doesn't mean poverty is completely..."

A woman speaks over gentle, rhythmic background music: "in those places. That means to make poverty history, we can't only rely on historical ways of measuring poverty. We are introducing higher standards for a growing world. Also, as..."

A person speaks in a clear voice, "As countries grow, their outlooks of what constitutes basic needs vary. While in one country, you may need just clothing and food to find work, in another, you may need a cell phone, a car, and access to internet in addition to food and clothing. Introducing a societal poverty line that combines extreme poverty, which is fixed, and a relative dimension of well-being that differs from country to country." This is all accompanied by rhythmic background music.

A woman speaks, "But poverty isn't all about money. To get a full picture, we need to understand that deprivation comes in many forms, and use a new multi-dimensional measure that not only considers income but also education, electricity, water, and sanitation. Finally..." The speech is accompanied by gentle, ambient music and the sound of typewriter keys being struck.

Soft background music plays as a woman speaks in a clear voice, "To expand our understanding of poverty, we need to go inside the household to learn how resources are shared. Globally, 104 women live in poor households for every 100 men. However, to know how many women are poor, we need to know how resources are shared within households. This requires more investments in survey research." This is followed by the sound of a pencil writing.

Uplifting orchestral music plays while a woman says, "It is possible to strive for a world in which all regions, countries, households, and people experience the benefits of poverty reduction. But for that, we need to piece together the poverty puzzle to understand its full impacts."
A gentle chime is followed by a resonant musical note.

audio_captions: A short piano melody plays.
A melodic, synthesized tune plays.
A gentle, melodic tune plays.
A male voice says, "This is Nokia Research Centre in Cambridge," followed by the sound of someone saying, "Uh..."
A man says, "Here we're looking at what nanotechnology can do for current mobile devices and what future mobile devices nanotech can enable," accompanied by soft electronic music.
Rhythmic, synthesized music plays.

Light, rhythmic electronic music plays as a character speaks, "Uh, nanomaterials are basically very small things that we think are going to have a big impact on mobile devices. So in terms of enhancing existing capabilities, but then also enabling totally new capabilities and new form factors."
A male voice says, "So let's start with hydrophobic surfaces."

A man speaks: "So I think most of us are probably familiar with what a hydrophobic surface is. So if you've got a Teflon coated frying pan at home, so you know that water really doesn't want to stick to a hydrophobic surface. Okay. So what we've got here is a little demo that's going to show you the difference between a regular hydrophobic surface and a super hydrophobic surface. So, if we think about what water does on a an uncoated surface, for instance, like the the edge of the the holder here. So it basically just wants to spread around on there. So now if we try it on the on the steel, so this has been coated with a low energy material. So now the the liquid really doesn't want to wet it, it kind of beads up like that and it will slide around. So this is just kind of a bit of fun so we can make a a marble maze using these materials. So the next thing I'm going to show you then is now we add some nanostructure to that same surface. So this is exactly the same except now we've got some very fine nanostructures on top of it. So now if I put the water on here, it behaves much differently, so it's much more mobile. So it's really difficult to control, much harder to solve the maze. So basically what's happening here is that the nanostructures are trapping a thin layer of air and the water is basically just sitting on that air layer and it's making it very, very mobile, so it's almost just like a like a liquid marble. And why why might you be interested in that in terms of a mobile device? Well, if we can put that over the electronics, for instance, then we've got a good chance that next time you drop it in the sink or in the bath, there's a good chance that it will survive because the water's not going to get to the sensitive electronics." This is all accompanied by a persistent, faint electronic hum and the sound of liquid sloshing.
Mysterious and slightly magical instrumental music plays.
A light, melodic piece of electronic music plays.
A man speaks, "What we have here is a demo that's going to show you some of these nanotechnologies. So we've got a phone." This is accompanied by gentle background music.
A male voice speaks, "So the Lumia 710 here is coated with one of these superhydrophobic surfaces." A low humming sound is present.

A man speaks, "It's got a nanostructured surface on there. What we're going to do is we're going to drop some water on the phone. It's going to bounce off." This is accompanied by a faint, continuous electronic sound.
A male voice speaks, "Underneath the phone here, there's a transparent sensor. So this has got a single atomic layer of".
A man speaks, "carbon on there, so it's got a patterned graphene layer that's been made into". This is accompanied by a low, humming sound.
A person speaks, "capacitive sensor. So that's going to detect the droplet impact and".
A person speaks, "I got the high-speed camera here sitting behind it." This is accompanied by a low, continuous humming sound.
A male voice says, "Okay, so let's take a look at what happened when that drop impacted the superhydrophobic surface. So here's the slow-mo movie."
A man speaks in a calm, clear voice, "So you get a bit of initial spread initially. And then the surface tension pulls it back in." This is accompanied by soft, ambient music.

A man speaks, "So if you do that on a regular surface, on the movie here you can see basically the the droplet would just stick to the surface. It's much less mobile. So in this case the things just all the pretty much all the waters bounced off on impact. It's not something new at all. No, I mean as ever, nature has already figured out these things. It's worked out millions of years ago through evolution that you can if you make a nanostructured surface which has got features on one length scale and then features on a much finer length scale and you combine those two things to make a kind of hierarchical structure. This is actually really good at resisting water. So things like the lotus leaf, also things like insect eyes and wings have these kind of structures on there, so they aggressively repel water and basically protect the the plant or the the insect." This is all accompanied by a subtle, ambient background sound.
A male voice speaks, "Ultimately, what we're hoping is that these nanotechnologies are enablers for". This is accompanied by soft, ambient electronic music.
A man speaks, "completely new device form factors. So if you think about maybe flexible devices, bendable devices, and ultimately maybe even stretchable devices." This is followed by a musical swell.

audio_captions: Upbeat electronic music plays in the background as a female voice speaks: "Scientists may have discovered a new cure for a very common illness. Researchers from the University of Southampton have discovered the specific gene called ADAM33. This gene causes asthma by narrowing people's airways. Apparently, ADAM33 forces the body to produce an enzyme that normally helps regrow damaged muscles. However, in people with asthma, it doesn't form properly and instead builds new muscles and blood vessels where it doesn't need to, and that narrows people's airways. Doctors define asthma as a chronic inflammatory disease of the airway. It causes the following symptoms: shortness of breath, tightness in the chest, coughing, and wheezing. Asthma can be mild, moderate, or severe, and it can vary from person to person. It can flare up from time to time and then not appear for long periods of time, or it can flare up every day. It just depends on who you are."

A female speaking in a high-pitched voice, "Scientists previously thought that the condition was mainly caused by allergens such as pollen or dust. And although that these things are not good for people with asthma, they don't actually cause asthma. Like I said before, scientists think that this new gene, ADAM33, makes people's airways narrower to begin with. The new study was recently published in the Journal of Clinical Investigations, which is a renowned scientific magazine. To get to this theory, scientists have experimented on both humans and mice to test the theory."

A female voice speaks, "Basically, they surrounded humans and mice with dust mites in hopes of activating the gene. Then they found out that if they could switch off ADAM33, asthma symptoms greatly decreased. Therefore, scientists now think that if you stop ADAM33 from malfunctioning, asthma could be prevented, though there is no way to do that just yet. On average, over 300 million people in the world suffer from asthma. This is a great medical advancement." This is accompanied by light, upbeat background music.

A person speaks, "packages because it's a double batch. It takes two packages. So it's one and a half cups of chopped up jalapenos with a cup of cider vinegar in the blender. The man laughs and continues, "It's true, they all seem to keep turning up on the music Friday playlist. How amazing is that? Anyway, it's time to open your door to Hack Music Theory." Background music plays.
A whooshing sound is followed by a man speaking in a deep voice, "The theory."

A woman speaks in a clear voice, accompanied by subtle background music: "A baseline is the foundation upon which all other melodies and chords are built. Therefore, a baseline has the dual purpose of functioning as your song's musical ground as well as its lowest melody. However, so many baselines these days only fulfill the former purpose, resulting in a solid foundation, but with no melodic interest. To achieve both of these roles simultaneously, use the theory hack from one by one, where rationale grounds his baseline into the root note of each chord before launching it into the melodic air for a few high notes." A swooshing sound is heard. "This creates an awesome two-in-one baseline that carries out both its foundation and melodic duties. The hack." Dramatic music then plays.

An upbeat, electronic musical track plays as a man speaks, "For the sake of this lesson, our example is very similar to the original song. Instead of copying the song though, have fun exploring how you can use this theory creatively with your own musical personality so it sounds like you." A woman says, "Step one, ground." The man continues, "Set up two bars of 4/4 with your grid set to 16th notes and your tempo set to 94 BPM. Next, you need to choose four chords from a minor key. The original song is in E minor, so we'll just stick with that. The chords we chose are E minor, G major, D major, and A minor." The woman says, "And by the way, if you need help with scales and chords, download our free book from hackmusictheory.com. Now, each chord is played over two quarter note beats." The man agrees, "Exactly. And the first beat will be used to ground into the root note, and the second beat will be used to fly away, but more on that in step two." The woman instructs, "Next, delete the second quarter note beat of each chord." The man says, "Like that," and there are sounds of a computer keyboard clicking. He continues, "And then over that first coordinate beat of each chord, play the root note a couple times with a rest in between," accompanied by more keyboard clicks. The woman says, "And this is what you'll end up with." The man explains, "And be sure to play one root note of each chord on an offbeat 16th note, like this one here. That's called syncopation and it's really going to add some extra groove." A simple electronic bassline is played. A swooshing sound is heard as the woman says, "Step two, air." The man explains, "Right, now that you've grounded your baseline, it's time to launch it into the melodic air. So, over the second quarter note beat of each chord, you could allow your baseline to break free of its low notes only restriction and elevate its range and melodic interest with some high notes." The woman instructs, "So, choose three ascending or descending notes from your scale and play them in a higher octave over your first chord." The man says, "Like this," followed by keyboard clicks. "And then do something similar over your third chord, like this," again with clicks. "And all of these are 16th notes, and also be sure to start on the offbeat 16th note for even more syncopation." The woman adds, "Then over your second chord, you're actually not going to go higher because that'll be too much of a good thing." The man says, "Exactly. So just add in a couple of low notes there, like this," followed by keyboard clicks. "And then finally, over your last chord, you're actually going to use the same three notes that you used over your third chord, but reverse their order, like this. Magic," accompanied by more clicks. The woman announces, "And now, it's time to have a listen to what we've made." The man concludes, "And if you want to keep learning how to make great music so you can get discovered, then we've got a video lined up on how to write better rhythms. So click that when it pops up in a few seconds, and we'll meet you there." An electronic music track with a prominent bassline and melody is played.

audio_captions: Upbeat electronic music plays in the background. A woman speaks in an energetic, fast-paced voice: "Hello you beauties out there in YouTube. How are you today? I'm Rebecca Foalgate and you are seeing my lovely round moon face for one reason. I am back with another most amazing top 10. Yes, it's that time of day where we rejoice and do top 10 things. So today we have a very exciting one. We have top 10 people with extra body parts. Ooh. So before I get launching in with that, guys, I have a question for you. Would you prefer to have three eyes or two mouths? Let me know in the comments below. Let me know. You have to choose. I think maybe three eyes. Why not? In at number 10, we have Tyson Smith, aka the guy with two hearts."
A thudding sound is heard, followed by a character speaking, "No, it isn't Doctor Who. It is Tyson Smith."

A rhythmic electronic beat and intermittent swooshing sound effects play as a woman speaks in a fast-paced, high-pitched voice: "Now, unfortunately, 36-year-old Tyson Smith from California had a heart defect and only months to live. To save his life, he had a piggyback heart transplant, which meant they put an extra heart into his body, allowing the two hearts to share the work. There is an incredible video of both hearts beating together, which has been watched a quarter of a million times on YouTube. This is insane, like, yes for technology and science. This isn't the only case of two hearts in one chest. A British girl named Hannah Clark had a similar surgery as a child, then had her original heart removed aged 16. She said this made her really happy, but she was left feeling a bit empty without two hearts. Incredible. Next up, meeting those two hearts but raising you a third leg, we have George Lippert in at number nine." A bell chimes. "Born in Bavaria in Germany in 1842, George Lippert had three fully formed legs and two functional hearts. At the age of 33, he started working for P. T. Barnum in the circus. He was billed as the original three-legged man. The original. His left leg was in perfect working order, his right leg was split into two legs, one of which had a foot with just three toes. Unfortunately, George died of tuberculosis in 1906."

Upbeat, rhythmic electronic music plays in the background as a woman speaks in a lively tone, "Getting kind of creepy here at number eight, we have Stelarc, the guy with an ear on his arm. Now, this isn't a natural ear. I hasten to add, this is an artificial ear right on his forearm. Crazy. Australian performance artist Stelarc had an extra ear grown on his forearm. Unable to find surgeons willing to create the arm ear, he had to wait over 10 years from when he first had the idea to having the procedure in 2007. He is now even pursuing surgery to have Wi-Fi installed in his arm ear so that the world can listen to what his arm ear is hearing. Can I say arm ear anymore? This is creepy. In regards to his third ear, Stelarc said, 'It's when art is surprising that it becomes interesting.' He wants the world to re-examine the body. Getting horny, but not in a good way here at number... we have Zhang Ruifang, aka the woman who grew a horn. Would we call a horn a body part? I guess if the person was a goat, then absolutely. But a Chinese woman has grown a horn. Wow. 104-year-old Zhang first started growing one horn at one side of her forehead at age 100. Now, the horn is officially known as a cutaneous horn, and it is made out of keratin, which is the same kind of protein we have in our nails. As one horn reached almost 3 inches, another started to grow on the opposite side of her face. So like, Zhang is pretty old and this happened when she was 100. Maybe this is just what happens at the next stage of human life. Like, you know, I guess back in the day when people started living to 30, some people were like, 'Whoa, gray hairs.' Maybe the next stage for humans is horns. Let me know what you think in the comments below. Here we are at number six, meet Bill Durks, the guy with two faces, two noses, and three eyes."

A female voice speaks, "Bill was born in Alabama in April 1913 and suffered from a condition known as frontonasal dysplasia. As a result of his deformity, he had two faces with two noses and a split cleft lip. This made him look like he had two faces and thus he became known as the man with two faces. Now this story has a bit of a sad twist, but don't worry, it has a happy ending. Because of his appearance, Bill was shunned from society and denied an education. At the age of 13, he joined a freak show where he painted on a third eye to make him look even stranger. He then became known as the man with three eyes. Now this is where things get good for Bill. He became very successful. People started flocking to come and see him. He made friends, he earned good money. The story has an even happier ending for him as he met his wife, Mildred the alligator-skinned woman, and they worked together in a show and lived together until their death. What a pair. Halfway at number five, meet Jasmine Tridevil, aka the woman with three boobs. Is three too many? I don't know. More than a handful is a waste, right? No, you haven't fallen asleep and woken up in Total Recall. This woman actually has three breasts. Count them. However, she wasn't born this way. 21-year-old dominatrix Jasmine had a prosthetic third breast built. She said she was rejected by 50 doctors who feared that they would be violating ethical codes. However, she eventually found one to perform the surgery. She says that medics took tissue from her stomach to build the breast. Now the reason she had the third breast is very interesting. She says, 'Sexually, I just didn't want to be approached by men anymore. So, I got a third breast to make myself feel unattractive. However, I still wanted to feel pretty.' I mean, whatever makes you happy, Jasmine. In at number four, we have the boy with 34 fingers and toes. Oh my goodness." All of this is accompanied by background music.

Upbeat electronic music plays as a woman speaks in a clear, fast-paced voice, "Akshat Saxena holds the Guinness World Record for having the most digits. With a condition known as polydactyly, Akshat has ten toes on each foot and seven fingers on each hand, bringing the total to 34. His mother, Amrita, said, 'I was so happy to see my baby as it was our first child, but later when I saw his fingers, I was shocked and surprised.' Now Akshat has since had surgery to remove his extra fingers and toes. I'm not sure whether I would do that though, because it was kind of cool. In at number three, we have Deepak Paswan, AKA the boy with eight limbs. Deepak Paswan from India was born with a parasitic twin on his stomach. The twin didn't survive, but the limbs absolutely did. Now, the most shocking thing about this is that the limbs continued to grow. So, as Deepak got older, the limbs got even bigger, and it literally looked like there was someone climbing inside his stomach. Deepak was born in a very poor village in India, and his family were unable to pay for the expensive and complex surgery that would be needed to save Deepak. After appealing for public help, the funds were raised, and he was able to have the operation. Before his surgery, people in the village would stare and gawk at him. Some even threw stones, saying he was the devil. Now, this story has a happy ending. The surgery was successful, and Deepak couldn't be happier. There's a lovely picture of him with his dad, and they just just look so happy. It's amazing. In at number two, getting pretty crazy, a baby was born with two heads. That's right. The two-headed baby was born in Bangladesh in November 2015. Thousands of people gathered at the hospital to see the baby, who was then shifted to intensive care. Now, the baby was born by cesarean, which was quite the shock for those delivering her. In order to protect her anonymity, her name hasn't been provided. Now, the baby is actually conjoined twin sisters who share the same body but have two heads. Now, this isn't the first situation of this kind. Abby and Brittany Hensel are two girls with one body, and they live a great life in Minnesota. Literally, they're walking around with one body, they have two heads. They were born in 1990, so they're in their mid-20s. They can now drive a car and have degrees. So, life can continue. These girls are an inspiration. So, we have reached that point in our most amazing top 10 people with extra body parts. The things we have seen, it has been incredible. To recap for you, we've had two hearts, we've had three legs, we've had ears on arms, we've had multiple faces, heads, and limbs. We've even had a horn. But what could possibly be at number one? For me, it is none other than Double Dick Dude. Wow! He's got two penises. Now, the reason for me he's at number one is because this isn't a case of a parasitic twin. There are no hidden extra body parts. This is two fully functioning penises, just there, two of them, twins."

A woman with an energetic voice speaks, "A guy known as Double Dick Dude posted about his rare condition on Reddit and verified it with a number of images. Now, these images we can't obviously show you in the YouTube video, but they are widely available on the internet if you want to Google it. Going by the name of Double Dick Dude because, obviously, his post on Reddit has attracted 17,000 comments. He then proceeded to conduct a Q&A on the site. Now, some of the answers are priceless. Popular questions were, 'Can you pee out of both penises?' And the answer was, 'Yes, but the double stream is a bit of a nightmare.' Others asked if both penises can get erect. Yes, they can. And some people have even asked if he has a favorite. He provides an answer. He prefers the right one, the left one's kind of mad about it. Now, this guy has even gone on to release a book called 'Double Header: My Life with Two Penises,' and the book was even a bestseller for Christmas 2014. I mean, what a guy! Like, I'm glad he decided to stick with them both. He is a very, very interesting man. So there we have it, that was our top 10 people with extra body parts. Very exciting. I feel like we've learned something. Like, I definitely have."
A brief burst of static is followed by a sustained, low-pitched electronic tone.

A female voice says, "Let me know what you thought in the comment section below. This is a really interesting topic, so I really want to read your comments. I'm Rebecca Felgate. This has been Most Amazing Top 10. Be sure to check out our other videos, like, share, and subscribe. I'll see you next time." This is all set to some light, upbeat background music.

audio_captions: Synthesized music plays, followed by the sound of applause.

The sound of applause is heard, followed by a woman speaking. "I love history, and especially that of invention. Since the arrival of Africans and African-descended people here in Boston in 1638, we have had black invention on these shores. The innovators that arrived many times did not have their names announced. They did not have the wherewithal to be able to secure patents. We hear names like Banneker, Grant, Latimer, even Brown. Some names we have not heard like Onesimus. He was the one who introduced inoculation here as an African in the 1700s. Banneker, the clock. We have innovators that have not been recognized, but we shall have."
A woman speaks, "... and innovator today that we will. There was a law that even forbid the patents for enslaved Africans to be received."
A person speaks, "When we think about, what is a patent? A patent".
A woman says, "is allowing the promotion and the process and the progress of art."

A person speaks, "of science and useful arts for the protection of the author, the writer or the inventor to use time allotted for that patent to be able to be licensed and to use it for sale. So when you are enslaved, you are property. So you may not have that right to do that. In fact, there was a commissioner, a US patent commissioner who made sure in 1857 that those who were enslaved would be denied the patent. Despite that, we have..."

A voice speaks, "had free African-Americans born even before that law came about. After the Patent Law of 1790 was announced, there was a man who was born the next year, 1791, who receives a patent as the first African-American to receive a patent in 1821. His name was Thomas Jennings. He received it for"

A woman speaks, "a dry scouring cleaning process. We all have on clothes today, and many of us have used dry cleaning. When we think about that, it is Thomas Jennings who came up with that process. He used the money from that patent to absolutely purchase his family. So, when we connect this idea of innovation and inventiveness with freedom in America, we have to look at what has slavery produced and how has this democratic process evolved with invention for those who have been denied its access. So, as we move forward, there's a particular and peculiar".

A woman with a clear voice speaks: circumstance in Massachusetts that happens to give us one of our most inventive and creative geniuses in America. It is Lewis Latimer that I am referring to, but the circumstances of his birth were not so smooth. His father was enslaved in Virginia. He escaped.

A person speaks, "self-liberated, self-emancipated, and ran to Boston in the 1840s as a way to be free. Once here, he was working and his former enslaver, Mr. Gary, heard that he was here and came to to capture him. He was returned to Virginia. The citizens of Massachusetts were enraged. And they decided that no one should be able to come to a free territory like Massachusetts and claim an enslaved, formerly enslaved person. And so they rallied. They met. And they created a petition that amassed 66,000 signatures. The petition even weighed 150 pounds. Can you imagine? It forced the Massachusetts legislature."
A person speaks, "to pass a personal liberties act in 1842. And so this Latimer petition was called the Great Massachusetts petition. Six years later, Lewis."

A woman speaks in a clear, steady voice, saying, "Latimer is born. George and Rebecca Latimer moved to Chelsea, Massachusetts after George Latimer's freedom was purchased for $400 from Mr. Gary. And they began a family. Lewis was born in 1848, and he was a bright child, industrious. He finished high school."

A woman speaks in a clear voice: "and went on to the US Navy. After his service in the Navy and honorable discharge, he decided to work in Boston. He was hired by a patent solicitor firm in Boston, Kater and Gould. And he was hired as an office boy in that room. He began to learn about drafting and drawing. And eventually, in a very short time as a matter of fact, he became a draftsman. He was so expert in his drafting that he gained the use of the office for his own practice and he was hired by Alexander Graham Bell to then do renderings of the telephone. Those actual drawings helped him to even improve the telephone. Thomas Edison heard about him and had him to do drafting of his invention of the light bulb, and it is here that we meet."

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "Latimer as an inventor who then establishes this use of a carbon filament to elongate the electric light. His first patent, you can see." A single musical note then plays.
A person speaks, "pictured here was a water trough for the railroad car and that first patent was 1874. His other patents ranged from 1881 to 1882, which gave not only a".

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "incandescent light bulb and its length in burning, but a support for the globe of the light bulb. He is accredited with at least seven patents in his life. And as he is going on in his career, he is hired by the US Electric Company."

A woman speaks in a clear, presentational tone: "He is then installing the lights in cities like New York, Philadelphia, Montreal, and London. He's on the board of the Thomas Edison Electric Company, and he joins General Electric in 1894. Here you see his picture with others who are on, uh, in that company, including women. I thought this was a very, uh, special photograph. Uh, as we..."

A female speaks, saying, "his work. He was a man of science and of literature. He wrote The Incandescent Electric Lighting. He wrote this volume of science that helps others to understand the electric process and lighting. And yet, he is not cornered or metered by that. He also has eloquence in words in a poem that I found that he..."

A woman speaks, "wrote to his wife called Ebony Venus. And so, we have a very magic man, I think, in the body of Lewis Latimer, who is only an example of the African genius and creativity of the innovator and innovators that had not been recognized in the history and the narrative of what we see in America and the world to raise the voice of the African-American in all branches of life. So, it is my pleasure to look at out at you and see light, to look up and see light, to be in Kendall Square and see light. And every time I see light, I'm going to think of Lewis Latimer, and I hope you will too. Thank you very much." The speech is followed by applause.
The sound of applause is followed by gentle, ambient music.

audio_captions: Upbeat electronic music plays in the background while a male speaker says, "The electrons shuffling around inside our computers move pretty fast. Theoretically, their top speed in silicon is up to 100,000 m per second. Which is good because the faster they can move, the faster chips can do calculations, the faster I can refresh Twitter. But there will always be something faster. Light. Why don't we use photons in computers instead of electrons? We already use photons for communication."
A person speaks in a clear voice, "Fiber optic cables are what keep the globe connected," accompanied by a low electronic hum.
A character speaks, "interconnected as they hurl data around at light speed."

A male voice speaks in a clear, informative tone: "But when it comes time to process that data, we convert light to electrons and run them through transistors. The conversion uses energy and electrons are comparatively slow, so researchers are exploring how to build light-based transistors instead. Transistors are the fundamental building block of your computer's central processing unit. They're basically nanoscale switches that will either stop current or let it flow. It's important that a transistor's output can act as the input for the next transistor. Actually, it has to be able to send the current on to at least two transistors for logic signals to propagate. And it has to preserve that signal quality to keep errors to a minimum. We have made optical switches, but for one reason or another, they don't work as a replacement for the silicon transistors we use in electronics. Like because the output signal is a different wavelength than the input, making controlling the next switch in line difficult. Or the design for the switch is too big in the micron scale instead of the nanoscale, so gains in speed come at the expense of size. Or the design requires a cloud of supercooled atoms, which isn't exactly practical." This is all set against a backdrop of light electronic music.

A male speaker with a clear voice says, "Even though scientists have been trying since the 60s, an optical transistor that can replace an electrical one has never materialized. like trying to build a photonic chip that mimics how a human brain performs calculations" over a subtle, rhythmic electronic beat. The speech is followed by a synthesized sound effect.

A male voice says, "Scientists at MIT have built a chip that uses beams of light sent through channels of silicon to mimic a neural network. The beams split and combine and travel at different speeds as the silicon is heated and cooled." This is accompanied by rhythmic electronic music.

A man speaks over gentle, futuristic electronic music: "Brighter beams represent bigger numbers. And as these beams split, combine, and interfere with each other, their brightness changes, effectively performing several small multiplication problems lightning fast." Subtle whooshing sound effects are heard.

A male character speaks in a clear voice over upbeat electronic background music, "They've applied this photonic chip to train a neural network to understand vowel sounds and have had modest success. They think they can improve their results dramatically by making a purpose-built system instead of the jury-rigged proof of concept they tested. But given how optical computing has historically failed to live up to expectations, skeptics aren't holding their breath. Before we see an all-light chip, we'll probably see hybrid opto-electronic systems that take advantage of light's ability to transmit data quickly across large distances. But until transistors reach their lower size limit and can't improve anymore, it looks like we'll be relying on slow old electrons to do the mathematical heavy lifting. We haven't found our way to the future of computing yet. So, make sure you're ready when we finally get there by starting your very own website with domain.com."

A man speaks, "domain.com is awesome, affordable, reliable, and has all the tools you need to build a new website. They can fulfill all your website needs. They offer .com and .net domain names and intuitive website builders. They have over 300 domain extensions to fit your needs from .ninja to .dog to .love. Take the first step in creating an identity online and visit domain.com." This is accompanied by upbeat background music.

A character speaks, "Why would transistors have a lower size limit? Well, you can blame quantum weirdness. Trace explains why we might one day ditch silicon here. Fun fact, there's a disagreement whether light-based computers or quantum computers are the future. But thanks to the nature of light, it's possible future computers could be both. Thanks for watching, and I'll see you next time on Seeker." This speech is accompanied by upbeat synthesized music, followed by a final synthesized flourish.

The man continues, "But for someone who two years ago was saying that it was laughable that Conor McGregor would be fighting a boxing great, and now he's 0-1 as a boxer and you're going to offer up arguably your best fighter to fight him, it seems a little disingenuous, it seems a little hypocritical. But of all people, Bob Arum, who is one of the loudest detractors of the Conor McGregor boxing experiment to do this, uh it's kind of funny. And I will also just add just to answer the question, I have no interest in this fight because I want to see Conor compete at what he's best at, which is MMA, and I want to see Terence Crawford compete at what he's best at, and that's boxing." Another man begins to speak, "Alright, and Ariel, everything that you said is true and I think that it is a little rich that Arum did it, but Audie Attar, Conor's manager came out and spoke on that same thing. A male voice speaks enthusiastically, "specifically is, are you interested? And I gotta tell you, I really am. Terence Crawford. I mean the X's and O's of this are just quite..."

A man speaks, "Conor likes to stand up when he fights. Okay, doing a stand-up fight with Terence Crawford doesn't seem like the world's greatest idea. Terence also has a wrestling background. A man speaks: "is left to discuss that these guys are going to go out and do an MMA fight under MMA unified rules. But if we can also agree that this is largely going to be a stand-up fight, I think it does get pretty interesting, pretty fast, and I will give a little credit where credit is due to Bob Arum for saying he wanted to do a two-fight deal. He wanted one MMA fight, one boxing fight, but he was willing to put MMA first because we always see the boxing guys come in and try to do this, but you never actually get to the MMA. Even when they try, you you've heard these ridiculous ideas where we're going to do it all in the same..." This is accompanied by upbeat music and intermittent swooshing sound effects.

A man speaks, "One round is MMA and the next round is boxing, but then when it's time to actually do the deal, the boxing round comes first and MMA is later and you never actually get to it. So I think that Arum offering this and saying they would come to the UFC first... I'm interested." Another man replies, "It does feel like progress. I I will give you that. It feels like progress in this debate of the MMA fighter boxing or the boxer going to MMA. To do a two-fight deal is something a little different and it does pique my interest a little more. Here's the other angle..."
A man speaks, "that people aren't really talking about. Uh, Dana White despises Bob Arum, and Bob Arum despises Dana White." Laughter is heard, and the man continues, "To put it mild."

A person speaks, "...right? Could those two actually sit at a table and do business? Now I know Dana White has a very good relationship with with Bob's son-in-law, Todd DuBoef over at Top Rank, so maybe he would get involved. But that's a real thing, right? Like that's a that's a big, that's a big hurdle in this, in this proposal, no?" Another person replies, "Oh yeah, Dana White called him and this was two years ago and I still remember it, a crusty old..." A brief laugh is heard. "...you'll have to look up how we finished that. But the point is, yeah, these guys aren't gonna..."

Two men engage in a discussion, accompanied by rhythmic, guitar-driven music. The first man speaks: "long and I think that Bob is pretty used to being the alpha male, particularly when it comes to fighting, and there's a new sheriff in town. So they're going to have to figure that out. I think Bob Arum's gonna have to come in with his hat in his hand a little bit more if he's going to do a deal with Dana White. I think he's starting to learn and realize that. But, I think that Bob brings something to the table here. I think that Terence Crawford is a real guy with real skills that's got a real fan base. I mean, there's something interesting there. Look, I'm not bullish on the fight that this is going to happen. That's not at all my message here. But you and I talking as two guys, I think it's a little fun. And I think if we hear more about Terence's wrestling background, I'll be more interested in it. I only heard that because people have said it. I'm a long-time wrestler, it's a small community. I've never seen this guy at a tournament, I've never seen this guy in a practice room. They're claiming that he has a wrestling background. But if he's got the courage to step into the Octagon with Conor McGregor, I'm gonna take him at his word." The second man responds: "Yeah, and I wonder if Terence is a big enough name, right? Like, I know he's a big name in the world of boxing. I don't know if he's, you know, a name like Floyd. I think it's fair, very fair to say that he's not a name like Floyd, but Conor is, you know, up there with Floyd as far as some of the, you know, the most famous athletes in the world. audio_captions: A female voice says, "Today, we're going to talk about the most dangerous animal of all time. Spoilers, it's not the honey badger." A light, playful instrumental piece begins and continues as she speaks again, "Hi, I'm Danielle Dufault and you're watching Animal Logic. Humans, or Homo sapiens, are the only extant members of the Hominina branch within the Great Ape family."

A character speaks in a clear voice, "You're probably wondering why we're talking about humans. After all, we have covered the chimpanzees, bonobos, and the gorillas, which are all part of the great ape family. But surprisingly, humans are actually very different from their ape relatives." A clicking sound is heard, and the speaker continues, "Okay, let's start with the physical." This is followed by another click. The speaker says, "Humans are sexually dimorphic, meaning that the males and females look different." After another click, the speaker continues, "The males are typically a bit larger with broad shoulders and narrow hips, while the females are typically a bit smaller with narrower shoulders and wider hips, which are useful in birthing children." A snapping sound is heard. The speaker concludes, "Unlike other apes, humans are fully bipedal, meaning they walk on two feet, and their bodies are not covered in fur. Though some humans may prove to be exceptions to the last one."
A female voice speaks, "cool. To make up for this lack of fur, humans had to develop what's called clothing, which started as animal furs and leathers and has evolved into cheap".

A woman speaks, "synthetic fabric that breaks down after a couple of uses, made by children in poor regions." A tapping sound is heard. She continues, "Humans also lack sharp claws and teeth. To make up for this shortfall, they've developed sharp sticks and clubs and..." A clicking sound is heard.

A female voice speaks, "Recently, remote-controlled aircraft equipped with deadly bombs." This is followed by a click sound. The voice continues, "Arguably, what has given them the biggest advantage over other animals is their massive brain in combination with their opposable thumbs, which allow them to easily use tools and send pictures of their genitals to prospective mates." After another click sound, the voice adds, "Homo sapiens are the latest in an evolutionary line that dates millions of years, though some believe that they've only been around for 6,000 years."

A female narrator says, "Throughout that process, Homo sapiens have moved around and evolved in different climates, giving them different skin tones and body features. They call these distinct physical characteristics race. And despite the fact that they are very smart creatures who've gone to the moon and put robots on Mars, they still find race to be an insurmountable issue that they continue to fight each other over every day." This is accompanied by a light instrumental track, with various sounds including a whoosh, paper rustling, and a pop.

A woman speaks in a clear, narrative voice: "Humans are one of the, if not the, most invasive species the Earth has ever seen, and they can be found on every continent on the planet." A clicking sound is heard. The woman continues, "While humans do have a relatively long gestation period, 9 months, development of disease-fighting antibiotics has caused the human population to skyrocket." Another clicking sound occurs. She goes on, "Most of them live in large, ecosystem-disrupting cities that grow larger and larger, polluting the environment more and more." A final click is heard, followed by her saying, "This massive growth and reckless disregard for the world they live in has seen the extinction of hundreds of other creatures and may very well one day lead to the extinction of humans themselves." The audio concludes with the sound of a rumbling explosion.

audio_captions: A man speaks, "I have two pieces of news for you."

Upbeat electronic music plays and continues in the background as a man says, "The first is that more than 1,000 experts in artificial intelligence and other sciences have signed an open letter arguing against the development of AI for warfare at the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence."
A male voice says, "The second is that there's an international joint conference on artificial intelligence," accompanied by background music.
Upbeat, modern background music plays as a male voice says, "This year's conference took place in Buenos Aires and focused on all things AI."
A man speaks, saying, "not just how robots could transform into dangerous weapons, but this particular story is really interesting." This is set against a backdrop of synthesized music.

A person speaks, "not just because it clearly lays out the case to stop AI weaponry before it starts, but also because of the people who have already signed it." This is accompanied by rhythmic background music.
A man says, "Those people include Tesla CEO, Elon Musk."
A male voice speaks, "ask Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak."
A voice states, "theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking."
...and MIT Professor Emeritus Noam Chomsky, among others.

A man speaks in an energetic voice, "If you scan the names and titles of the people attached to this letter, you'll recognize more than a few organizations represented. There are people from Google, Microsoft, and hundreds of universities on the list." This is all accompanied by upbeat electronic music.
A man speaks in a clear voice, "These are some seriously smart people. So, what are they so concerned about?"
A male voice speaks, "the main focus of the letter is how weaponized artificial intelligence could create a new global arms race." This is accompanied by a subtle, low-frequency electronic tone.
A man speaks, saying, "one that would result in a very dangerous situation for millions of people." This is accompanied by a low, humming sound.
A man says, "As the letter says, autonomous weapons have been described as the third revolution in warfare after gunpowder and nuclear arms." This is accompanied by rhythmic electronic music.
A person speaks, "It goes on to say that if these technologies are pursued..."
A male voice states, "A global arms race is virtually inevitable and the end point of this technological trajectory is obvious," accompanied by electronic music.

A man speaks, "autonomous weapons will become the Kalashnikovs of tomorrow. So just imagine a cold war that is waged not with the build-up of nuclear weapons, but with armed robots." This is accompanied by light, synthesized background music.
A male voice says, "Now, if you're looking at warfare as a necessary evil, an autonomous army seems like a great choice," accompanied by a low, rhythmic whirring sound.

A male voice speaks, "It means you don't put your own people at risk. But that might also mean that it lowers your threshold for entering into a conflict. You might be more willing to use force because the stakes on your side are so low." This is accompanied by light electronic music.
A person speaks, "So there's a fear that these robots could make war easier and more frequent, not to mention," accompanied by rhythmic electronic music.
A male voice speaks, "What might happen if terrorists or oppressive leaders got hold of the technology?"

A male voice speaks, "The letter also makes a point to stress that AI has enormous benefits to humanity. So it's not a warning about Skynet or anything like that." This is accompanied by electronic music.

A character speaks in a clear voice, "Also, nearly every story I've seen talking about this uses a picture of the Terminator robot as art. I'm not going to do that. So here's a picture of Johnny 5 from Short Circuit 2." This is all accompanied by a low, electronic whirring sound.
Electronic dance music is playing.

A male voice speaks energetically, accompanied by subtle electronic music: "Guys, if you enjoyed this video, why not hit the like button down there? And you can keep up with the coolest news in science, tech, pop culture, and just about everything else by subscribing to this channel. Doing so is guaranteed to make you sound smarter. Not an actual guarantee."
A low, humming sound.

Another important step in the operation of your fireplace is to adjust the flame height and therefore the heat output. Many of our fireplaces have a remote control that accomplishes this for you simply by pushing an up or down arrow. Some of our fireplaces, such as this one, have a manual control which you access in the controls area of the fireplace. The man then says, "Now that we've removed the decorative front, we can see the knob to adjust the heat output and flame height is labeled high and low. There may be a slight delay when the fan turns on and off. This is because the fans operate with either a timer or a heat sensor. This prevents cold air being blown into the room on startup and also maximizes heating by continuing to blow warm air from around the fireplace after it is turned off." audio_captions: A piece of music is played on a string instrument.

A man speaks in a calm, informative voice against a backdrop of gentle, melodic music and the sound of birds chirping: "When putting in a bird-friendly garden, it's tempting to use those big, showy native plants like the large flower. However, it's really important that we grow diverse gardens that provide habitat for a lot of the smaller Australian birds as well. We need to put in some spiky leaf plants, and a perfect example is this prickly Moses, which provides perfect sort of protection for a lot of those smaller Australian birds for their day-to-day life as well as for their nesting." Twinkling chimes are heard. The man continues, "Prickly Moses, Acacia ulicifolia, is a perfect example of a locally native wattle for the Sydney region that's fantastic for helping out our small birds. Insects are attracted to its flowers, and these are a food source for small insect eaters. And its prickly foliage also provides shelter for species such as the superb fairy-wren and silvereye. The spiky cover also makes it a great nesting site for small birds like the red-browed finch."
A synthesized musical piece plays.

Gentle music plays as a man speaks, "This plant grows well in temperate and subtropical areas of Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, and Tasmania. It's perfect for informal screening, and while its prickly foliage makes it an ideal habitat plant for small birds, it is very spiky. So avoid planting it where there's lots of foot traffic or consider planting a row of shrubs in front of it as a barrier. Many of these spiky-leafed shrubs are understory plants that grow under big gum trees in their natural habitat. So they're perfectly happy in a bit of light shade in your garden. But when they're given full sun, they can really become showy feature plants. The Prickly Moses has masses of these small, ball-shaped wattle flowers as well as the prickly foliage. And it really adapts well to quite a wide range of soil types provided you've got reasonable drainage. And it'll grow to a useful height of about 1.5 to 3 meters where the birds can really access it." The speech is accompanied by the sounds of birds chirping and insects buzzing.

Gentle, melodic music plays as a man speaks, "Acacias belong to the legume family, which means that they have bacteria in their roots that are able to fix nitrogen from the air and use it as a nutrient. As a result, they're great pioneer plants for starting off your gardens. They grow quickly and don't need to be fertilized. Another great reason to include them in your garden. Unlike most woody Australian plants, wattles do not usually respond well to heavy pruning. To be on the safe side, it's a good rule of thumb not to cut into wood any thicker than a pencil. But if they do get a bit leggy, you might want to give them a light trim. But make sure that you wear gloves and long sleeves because the prickly foliage can sometimes cause allergic reactions to your skin. The spiky foliage of prickly Moses provides the perfect option for creating protection for our small birds. But growing a bird-friendly garden is more than just putting in one or two plants. To provide the complete habitat for a whole range of birds, we need layers, from ground covers to small and medium shrubs, and even trees if you've got the space. For more ideas, go to the creating places page on the Birds in Backyards website. Enjoy the journey." The sound of birds chirping can also be heard.
The sound of a bird chirping is heard, accompanied by other birds singing and insects buzzing. This is followed by a frog croaking.

audio_captions: Upbeat electronic music plays. A man speaks, "Hey, I'm Nate and today we're checking out the rugged Cat B15Q. Now the phone comes to us from Caterpillar."
A person speaks, "a company that's probably better known for those big yellow construction vehicles," accompanied by background music.

A man speaks, "I doubt this is going to be able to stand up to quite as much punishment as those behemoths, but it's definitely built to last and starts at $350 unlocked." Upbeat electronic music begins to play. A different man then says, "The specs here aren't really impressive. The 4-inch screen has a measly 800 by 480 pixel resolution and doesn't hold up too well in direct sunlight. Viewing angles aren't great either. Colors look fine, but hold the phone at the wrong angle and the contrast degradation becomes really noticeable."

A male speaker says, "There's also only four gigs of total storage space. It does have a microSD card slot though, with support for up to 32 gig cards, so you're going to want to pick one up if you plan on installing many apps. Performance on the other hand isn't bad. A 1.3 gigahertz quad-core CPU isn't all that stellar on paper, but the phone never got in the way as I flipped through apps and websites during my testing. More importantly, simpler casual games like Angry Birds Transformers handle really well, so any downtime can be spent productively. There's a 5-megapixel camera on the back." This is all accompanied by upbeat background music.
A man speaks in a conversational tone, "And while I was able to tease out the occasional usable shot in ideal conditions, bright lighting, that sort of thing..."

A person speaks, saying, "It mostly cranks out grainy, noisy shots. The autofocus is also pretty sluggish, so you're going to want to stick to slow-moving or static objects." This is accompanied by a rhythmic, electronic beat.

Upbeat electronic music plays as a male speaker says, "But you probably aren't buying a rugged smartphone for gaming and photography. This thing is solid with a scratch-resistant Gorilla Glass 2 display. It's also pretty light, just under 6 oz. That's thanks to the silver anodized aluminum body."
A man speaks, "Rubber bumpers keep the corner safe and also make sure the phone is really comfortable to hold. The B15Q is IP67 certified." This is accompanied by light background music.
A male voice speaks, "That means it's dustproof and waterproof."
A male voice speaks clearly, "In this case, up to 3 ft for 30 minutes. The phone's USB port and headphone jacks are covered."
A male voice speaks clearly, "And you'll get a little warning when unplugging the phone or removing the headphones, reminding you to seal it back up. It's a pretty nice touch."
A man speaks, "Now on the back, you'll find the locking switch." followed by a click.
A clicking sound is heard, followed by a person speaking, "Slide that over to the right and you'll see the yellow. That means it's unlocked."

A person speaks, "And then you're going to pry the back plate off. It's a little tough to get off, which is a good thing actually because that's how the phone keeps its water resistance. Underneath, you'll find the 2,000 milliamp-hour battery."
A person says, "the micro SD card slot and the SIM card slot," accompanied by light electronic music.
A person says, "This particular model has dual SIM."

Electronic music plays as a person speaks, "So that's the CAT B15Q. Now if you're just a little clumsy, this phone is probably going to be overkill, especially at $350. But if you work outdoors or spend a lot of time camping and are worried about, you know, dropping your phone or inclement weather, this is gonna be a pretty strong contender. The glossy display does give me pause though, so you're going to want to be wary if you spend a lot of time in bright sunny areas. I'm Nate Ralph, thanks for watching." The music continues to play.
